sections: Audit Program Management and Business Applications
reqs: Tell apart product, service, process, desk, department, function, element, system, management, combined, joint, hybrid and remote audits, and pick the one that fits a situation.
Classify an audit as first-, second- or third-party and as internal or external from who performs it and on whose behalf.
Distinguish CAPA verification, risk-based, registration, compliance, surveillance and for-cause audits by the reason they are carried out.
Apply the purposes, evidence-gathering techniques and tracing methods that quality audits share with sustainability, environmental, safety and financial audits.
Write a clear audit purpose and set a scope (processes, locations, time period) that follows from it.
Explain how independent audits show management the effectiveness and efficiency of the system and expose financial, cybersecurity and other risks.
Identify and rank the criteria an audit compares evidence against: industry, national and international standards, contracts, quality agreements, specifications, policies and the internal QMS.
Roles and responsibilities of audit participants
Assign the right duties to the lead auditor, team members, client, auditee, observers, guides and technical experts.
Apply the spirit of the ASQ Code of Ethics, due diligence and due care, confidentiality and conflict-of-interest rules, and respond correctly to illegal acts or unsafe conditions.
Recognize how careless or negligent auditing creates legal and financial exposure, and how audit records can affect the auditee's liability.
Protect audit credibility through auditor independence, objectivity and qualifications.
Elements of the audit planning process
Work through the basic planning steps: confirm authority, set purpose, scope, type and format, pick the criteria, map process boundaries and size the team and documentation.
Weigh education, experience, industry background, technical expertise and independence when choosing auditors for a given audit.
Find and use pre-audit information such as criteria references, gap assessments and prior audit results to focus the audit.
Arrange safety, security, escorts, confidentiality, right of access and facilities such as workspace, internet and PPE before the audit.
Choose a sampling plan and method, prepare checklists, log sheets and forms, and decide whether records will be kept on paper or electronically.
Pick and use forward tracing, backward tracing, discovery and observation to suit what the audit needs to show.
Build an audit plan from planning information and share it with the client, auditee and other stakeholders.
On-site audit management for the auditor
Manage time on site, adjust team activities and resources, revise the plan when needed and keep the auditee informed as the audit proceeds.
On-site audit management for the auditee
Act for the auditee as liaison and guide, supply clarifying information and confirm or dispute findings during the audit.
Run an opening meeting that covers purpose, scope, grading criteria, attendance, the schedule and attendee questions.
Gather information by interview, observation, measurement and document review, and judge how much each piece counts as evidence.
Tell objective evidence from opinion and recognize evidence that is observed, measured, confirmed, corroborated or documented.
Rank evidence by significance, severity, frequency and risk, judge its impact including on cost of quality, and decide whether more investigation is needed.
Run the closing meeting: restate the basis of the audit, record attendance, present results, get agreement on the facts and settle next steps and owners.
Turn audit observations into clear, actionable findings, judge their significance, severity and risk, and build the report so critical issues stand out and each finding can be tracked.

Design and judge an audit report with background, an executive summary and prioritized results, present conclusions clearly with suitable analytical tools, and set a timeline for responses and corrective action.
Get the report approved and distributed as the procedure requires, and assemble and retain the audit file according to policy.
Elements of the corrective and preventive action (CAPA) process
Judge whether a CAPA response contains the essential elements: a responsible owner, real root cause analysis, and action that prevents recurrence.
Review of corrective and preventive action (CAPA) plan
Decide whether a proposed CAPA and its schedule are acceptable and negotiate changes when they are not.
Verification of corrective and preventive action (CAPA)
Verify that a CAPA was implemented and is effective by checking revised procedures, observing changed processes and running follow-up audits.
Follow-up on ineffective corrective and preventive action (CAPA)
Choose and plan the right response when CAPA is not implemented or does not work, such as escalation, a reissued request or a re-audit.
Apply the criteria and steps needed to formally close an audit.
Recognize the personal traits that make an auditor effective and apply lead auditor skills such as negotiating and directing a team around members' strengths and weaknesses.
Manage the audit team, meetings, activities and logistics on site, adjusting the plan when conditions change.
Analyze conflict situations during an audit, from disagreements to delaying tactics and interruptions, and choose the right technique to resolve them.
Choose and evaluate written, oral and electronic communication and the right charts, graphs and diagrams for audit meetings and reports across local, global, remote and multi-site settings.
Select and use questioning, listening and prompting techniques to gather reliable evidence in interviews, including with supervisors present, in groups and through translators.
Build, facilitate and lead audit teams, and recognize and respond to each stage of team development.
Explain how senior management establishes the audit function and supports it with authority, resources and action on results.
Build and judge audit staffing budgets that cover auditor and auditee time, choose special arrangements such as contracted, shared or integrated audits, and adjust resources from results.
Set minimum auditor knowledge and skills, plan training in audit methods, standards, regulations, diversity and facilitation, and define continuing education.
Choose metrics that show whether the audit program is effective, including its effect on cost and on organizational risk.
Design internal audit policies, procedures, schedules and review cycles, and use periodic reviews to find systemic trends and recommend improvements for emerging risks.
Design a supplier audit program, including qualification surveys, surveillance audits, self-assessments and supplier improvement work.
Use audit results to find good practices and lessons learned and to standardize them across the organization.
Analyze how the audit program and organizational risk affect each other, and assess preparedness through business continuity and succession planning.
Summarize audit program results, trends and changes in risk into useful input for management review.
Electronic records and computerized system considerations
Detect data integrity, fraud and cybersecurity issues in electronic records and computerized systems, and know when to evaluate retention, retrieval and electronic document control.
Use audit results and performance data to monitor improvement, suppliers, customer satisfaction and metrics, and give management an independent view of strategy deployment.
Recognize how business units and sites connect and how their separate metrics and goals can conflict.
Classify costs into the four COQ categories and analyze how the audit program shifts them.

Identify, read and analyze the classic quality tools (Pareto, cause and effect, flowcharts, control charts, check sheets, scatter diagrams, histograms), root cause analysis such as 5 whys, and the PDCA cycle, and judge whether an auditee has used them correctly.
Recognize the Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve and Control phases, what each one delivers, and apply them when reviewing or supporting an improvement project.
Apply lean principles and tools (5S, standardized work, kanban and pull, error-proofing, value stream mapping and the 8 wastes) to spot and judge improvement opportunities.
Value stream map and takt time
Calculate and interpret the mean, median and mode, and choose the one that best describes a given data set.
Calculate and interpret standard deviation and build and read a frequency distribution.
Describe qualitative data by type, turn it into countable data by coding or grouping, and use quantitative data to see patterns and trends and tell a systemic problem from an isolated one.
Data collection plan and check sheet
Tell common cause variation from special cause variation and know which kind of response each one calls for.
Explain what goes into Cp and Cpk (centering, stability, specification limits, distribution) and how capability studies and related metrics support quality goals.
Define outliers, judge their significance and effect on process performance, and use methods such as the IQR rule and box plots to find them.
Use single and double attributes plans and variables plans to make lot acceptance decisions and understand their tradeoffs.
Choose between random, stratified and cluster sampling, and know the uses and limits of non-statistical sampling, including risk-based sampling and the effect of measurement system quality.
Explain consumer's risk, producer's risk and confidence level and how they shape sampling decisions.
Recognize the principles of change control and configuration management for hardware, software (including security), products, processes and services, and what audit evidence shows they work.
Tell verification from validation, know who is qualified to do them, and judge whether suitable methods were used.
Describe risk responses (avoidance, mitigation, tradeoffs) and tools for estimating and controlling risk: FMEA, PFMEA, DFMEA, HACCP, CTQ analysis and SWOT.
Voice of the customer to CTQ tree
bank: I.A.1
A plant pulls five boxed valves from finished goods after final inspection, takes them apart and checks them against the drawing and the customer's order. What type of audit is this?
Process audit
System audit
Desk audit
Product audit

A product audit re-examines finished product that has already been accepted to confirm it meets requirements. A process audit would look at how the work is done, its methods and parameters, rather than at the finished item.
std
I.A.1
What best distinguishes a product audit from routine final inspection?
It checks every unit before shipment so that bad parts are sorted out
It re-checks accepted product to judge the controls
It is carried out only by the customer at its own receiving dock
It replaces final inspection once the process has been shown capable
A product audit samples product that has already passed inspection to find out whether the system that produced and accepted it is working. Sorting every unit is the job of inspection, not an audit.
std
I.A.1

A hotel group's quality staff stay as ordinary guests at one property and rate check-in time, room cleanliness against the brand standard and how a staged complaint is handled. Which audit type is this?
Service audit
Product audit
Management audit
Desk audit

A service audit evaluates how a service is delivered to the customer against its requirements. A product audit examines a tangible output, while here the output is the guest's experience of the service.
std
I.A.1

An auditor watches a heat-treat operation, compares furnace temperature and soak time with the work instruction, and checks the operators' training records and the calibration of the thermocouples. What type of audit is this?
Process audit
Product audit
Element audit
Management audit

A process audit checks that a process runs as planned, looking at its inputs, methods, parameters, people and equipment. An element audit would follow one requirement such as calibration across many areas instead of one process end to end.
std
I.A.1

A company passes its system audits every year, but defects keep escaping from one welding cell. The quality manager wants to know whether the cell really runs to its procedure and set parameters. Which audit fits best?
Another full system audit of the QMS against the ISO 9001 clauses
A desk review of the welding procedure and related documents only
A process audit of the welding cell against its procedure and parameters
A management audit of how senior leaders set the plant's business strategy

The question is about how one process actually runs, so a process audit that observes the cell and checks its parameters is the right tool. Another system audit would cover the whole QMS at a broad level and could easily miss what happens in that one cell.
std
I.A.1
A buyer sends a new supplier a questionnaire about its quality system, asks for its quality manual and certificates, and evaluates the replies without visiting. What type of audit is this?
Remote audit
Desk audit
Third-party audit
Product audit

A desk audit is a document- or questionnaire-based assessment with no on-site or live activity. A remote audit uses technology to interview people and observe work in real time, which the buyer is not doing here.
std
I.A.1
What is the main limitation of a desk audit of a supplier?
It cannot be used to screen a supplier before a contract is signed
It shows what documents say, not whether practice matches them
It requires a certified lead auditor and a full audit team to run
It takes more time and money than a full on-site audit of the supplier

A desk audit reviews documents and self-reported answers, so it cannot confirm that the work is actually done that way. It is in fact a common, low-cost way to screen suppliers before a contract, so that option is backwards.
std
I.A.1
An audit covers every applicable requirement within the shipping department only: document control, training, handling, packaging and records. What type of audit is this?
Department audit
Element audit
System audit
Product audit
A department audit looks at all the requirements that apply within one organizational unit. An element audit would do the opposite, following a single requirement across many departments.
std
I.A.1
An auditor examines how purchasing is carried out wherever it happens: by buyers at headquarters, at two plants and at a field service depot. What type of audit is this?
Department audit
Function audit
Product audit
Desk audit

A function audit follows one business function, here purchasing, wherever it is performed, even across several departments and sites. A department audit is bounded by one organizational unit, so it would not reach buyers spread across the company.
std
I.A.1
An auditor checks the document control requirements in every department of a plant, from engineering to maintenance. What type of audit is this?
Element audit
Department audit
Process audit
Management audit
An element audit takes one element or clause of the criteria and checks it horizontally across the organization. A department audit would instead cover all requirements within a single department.
std
I.A.1

Last year each internal audit covered one department in full. This year the audit program manager wants to know how calibration control is working throughout the plant. What change best meets her need?
Repeat the department audits with larger samples taken in each department
Plan an element audit that follows calibration control through every area
Run a product audit on parts that were measured with calibrated gauges
Schedule a management audit of the budget for calibration services

Following one requirement across all areas is an element (horizontal) audit, which gives a plant-wide view of calibration. Repeating department audits would still spread calibration across many separate audits and would not give that focused view.
std
I.A.1

Before its certification audit, a company's internal team checks whether all of its QMS processes and their interactions meet ISO 9001 and are implemented across the organization. What type of audit is this?
Element audit
Process audit
System audit
Product audit

A system audit evaluates the whole management system, its processes and how they interact, against the criteria. Element and process audits look at one requirement or one process, which is narrower than what is described.
std
I.A.1
The board asks for an audit of how well senior leaders' policies, decisions and use of resources are achieving the company's quality objectives. What type of audit is this?
System audit
Management audit
Department audit
Process audit

A management audit evaluates management's own performance, such as policies, decisions and resource use, against the objectives they are meant to achieve. A system audit checks that the QMS processes conform and are implemented, rather than judging leadership's decisions.
std
I.A.1
A company certified to both a quality and an environmental management standard has one audit team cover both systems in a single audit. What is this called?
A joint audit
A hybrid audit
An element audit
A combined audit
A combined audit covers two or more management systems of one auditee together. A joint audit is different: it is two or more auditing organizations auditing the same auditee.
std
I.A.1
Two customers that buy from the same supplier agree to send their auditors together and carry out one audit of the supplier. What is this called?
A combined audit
A third-party audit
A joint audit
A desk audit

A joint audit is one audit of a single auditee by two or more auditing organizations. A combined audit is one auditee audited against two or more management system standards, which is not what happens here.
std
I.A.1
The lead auditor works on site while a technical expert joins by video from another country to review design records with the engineers. What format is this audit?
Remote
Joint
Hybrid
Combined
A hybrid audit mixes on-site and remote activities in the same audit. It is not fully remote, because part of the team and part of the work are physically on site.
std
I.A.1
Travel restrictions prevent any site visit, so the whole audit is done by video call, with shared screens for records and a live camera walk of the shop floor. What type of audit is this?
Desk audit
Hybrid audit
Remote audit
Joint audit

A remote audit uses technology to interview people, view records and observe work in real time from another location. A desk audit only reviews documents or questionnaires and has no live observation.
std
I.A.1
During a remote audit, the live video of the production floor keeps dropping, and the auditee offers to email photos of the area instead. What should the lead auditor do?
Accept the photos as equal to direct observation of the work in that area
Cancel the whole audit at once and reschedule it later as an on-site visit
Conclude that the area conforms, since no problems were seen on the video
Record the limitation and plan an on-site or later live check of that area

When technology prevents reliable evidence, the gap should be recorded and the area verified another way. Photos chosen by the auditee are weaker evidence than live observation, and cancelling the whole audit is out of proportion to a problem in one area.
std
I.A.2
A company's own internal audit team audits its machining department against company procedures. How is this audit classified?
First-party, internal
Second-party, external
Third-party, external
Second-party, internal
An organization auditing itself is a first-party audit, which is an internal audit. Second-party audits are done by a customer or other interested party on a supplier, so they are external.
std
I.A.2
Auditors from a pump maker visit a casting supplier to judge whether it can meet the pump maker's requirements. How is this audit classified?
First-party, internal
Third-party, external
First-party, external
Second-party, external

A customer auditing its supplier is a second-party audit, external to the supplier. It is not third-party, because the pump maker has a direct interest in the outcome rather than being independent of both sides.
std
I.A.2
A company hires an outside consultant to carry out its internal audits against its own QMS. How are these audits classified?
First-party, because they are done on behalf of the company
Third-party, because the consultant is independent of the company
Second-party, because the consultant is paid by the company
Joint, because two organizations take part in the same audit

Who the audit is done for decides the classification: internal audits remain first-party even when an outsider performs them on the organization's behalf. Third-party audits are done by an independent body such as a certifier or regulator for purposes outside the organization.
std
I.A.2
A customer pays an independent auditing firm to audit one of its suppliers against the customer's requirements. How is this audit classified?
Second-party
Third-party
First-party
Internal

An audit performed by others on behalf of a customer is still a second-party audit, because it serves the customer's interest. The firm's independence does not make it third-party; third-party audits serve purposes such as certification or regulation.
std
I.A.2
A certification body audits a company's QMS to decide whether to issue an ISO 9001 certificate. How is this audit classified?
Second-party
Third-party
First-party
Internal

A certification body is independent of both the organization and its customers, which makes this a third-party audit. A second-party audit is done by or for a customer with a direct stake in the supplier.
std
I.A.2
Why do many customers accept a supplier's third-party certificate in place of some of their own audits?
Third-party auditors review every requirement in each customer's contracts
Third-party audits always find more problems than customer audits do
The certifier is independent and audits to a common standard
The supplier chooses which areas the certifier is allowed to examine

Third-party certification gives an independent check against a shared standard, which saves customers from repeating the same basic audit. It does not cover each customer's specific contract requirements, which is why customers may still do some second-party audits.
std
I.A.2
Which statement correctly contrasts internal and external audits?
Internal audits use company staff; external audits must use hired consultants
Internal audits are first-party; external audits are second- or third-party
Internal audits check procedures; external audits check only finished product
Internal audits are optional; external audits are required by ISO 9001

The internal or external context follows the relationship: first-party audits are internal, and second- and third-party audits are external. Who carries out the work does not decide it, since a consultant can perform an internal audit on the organization's behalf.
std
I.A.3

Three months after a supplier reports it fixed a labeling error, the customer's auditor returns to confirm that the new label check is in place and that no mislabeled lots have shipped since. What kind of audit is this?
A CAPA verification audit
A surveillance audit
A registration audit
A risk-based supplier audit

The audit exists to confirm that a specific corrective action was implemented and worked. A surveillance audit is a periodic check by a certification body that a certified system is still maintained, not a check on one action.
std
I.A.3

An audit program manager sets audit frequency and depth by the likelihood and consequence of process failures, so the sterilization process gets far more audit time than the mailroom. What approach is this?
Compliance auditing
For-cause auditing
Risk-based auditing
Surveillance auditing
Allocating audit effort according to risk is risk-based auditing. For-cause audits respond to a specific event such as a failure, whereas this is planned allocation across the whole program.
std
I.A.3
A company that has never been certified invites a certification body to determine whether its QMS can be certified to ISO 9001. What kind of audit is this?
A surveillance audit
A compliance audit
A for-cause audit
A registration audit
A registration audit is the initial third-party audit used to decide whether to grant certification. Surveillance audits come later, to confirm that a certified system is still being maintained.
std
I.A.3
What decision is a registration audit mainly designed to support?
Whether to approve a single supplier's first shipment
Whether to grant certification to a standard
Whether a corrective action fixed a past nonconformity
Whether a product lot may be released to the customer

A registration audit gives the certification body the evidence it needs to decide whether to certify the system. Checking a single corrective action is the purpose of a CAPA verification audit, not a registration audit.
std
I.A.3
One year after a company was certified, the certification body returns to sample parts of the QMS and confirm it is still maintained. What kind of audit is this?
A registration audit
A surveillance audit
A for-cause audit
A CAPA verification audit

Surveillance audits are periodic, usually partial-scope audits that keep a certification in force between full audits. A registration audit is the initial certification audit, which the company has already passed.
std
I.A.3
An audit at a food plant checks that sanitation records, allergen labels and temperature logs meet the applicable government regulations. Which purpose does this audit serve?
Compliance
Management review
Risk-based scheduling
Surveillance

A compliance audit checks conformity to set requirements, here legal and regulatory ones. Surveillance refers to a certification body's periodic visits to maintain a certificate, which is not what is described.
std
I.A.3
After a sudden rise in field failures traced to one supplier's lots, the customer schedules an unplanned audit of that supplier's process. What kind of audit is this?
A surveillance audit
A for-cause audit
A registration audit
A desk audit
A for-cause audit is triggered by a specific problem or event rather than by the regular schedule. A surveillance audit is planned and periodic, not a response to a failure.
std
I.A.3
How does a compliance audit differ in emphasis from an audit focused on system effectiveness?
It checks conformity to rules rather than results achieved
It looks only at finished product rather than at the processes behind it
It is carried out only by government agencies rather than by companies
It relies on interviews alone rather than on records and observation

A compliance audit asks whether stated requirements, often legal or contractual, are being met. An effectiveness focus asks whether the system achieves its intended results; both can use the same evidence-gathering methods.
std
I.A.3

An audit program follows a fixed annual schedule. A new product launch has introduced unproven processes, and a recent customer complaint points to one of them. What should the audit program manager do?
Keep to the schedule, since changing it would weaken audit independence
Wait for the next scheduled system audit to cover the new processes
Add a for-cause audit and raise the audit priority of the new processes
Ask the process owners to audit their own new processes this month

A complaint justifies a for-cause audit, and new, unproven processes carry higher risk, so a risk-based program should give them more attention. Holding to the original schedule ignores the change in risk, and independence is not harmed by rescheduling.
std
I.A.4
A quality auditor joins an environmental audit team for the first time. Which of her skills carries over most directly?
Interpreting quality standard clauses on design and development
Measuring parts against drawing dimensions and tolerances
Classifying product defects as critical, major or minor
Interviewing, observing and reviewing records

Evidence-gathering techniques such as interviews, observation and record review are common to all audit disciplines. The other skills are tied to quality-specific criteria that do not apply to an environmental audit.
std
I.A.4
A financial auditor picks a recorded payment and follows it back to the invoice, the receiving record and the purchase order. Which quality audit technique matches this?
Forward tracing
Backward tracing
Discovery method
Element sampling
Starting from a result and following it back toward its source is backward tracing, used the same way in quality audits. Forward tracing runs the other way, from the source toward the output.
std
I.A.4
In an environmental audit, the auditor starts where a hazardous waste is generated and follows it through storage and shipping papers to the final disposal record. Which technique is this?
Backward tracing
Desk review
Element sampling
Forward tracing
Following material from its origin through each step to the final record is forward tracing. Backward tracing would start from the disposal record and work back toward the source.
std
I.A.4
In a safety audit, the lockout records for a press are complete. Why should the auditor also watch a technician perform lockout?
Records show what was reported, not always what is done
Safety audits cannot use records as evidence of any kind
Watching the work is faster than reviewing the lockout records
Observation removes the need to interview the technician

Combining record review with direct observation is a basic technique in every audit discipline, because records alone may not reflect practice. Records are valid safety audit evidence; they are just not enough by themselves.
std
I.A.4
An auditor is asked to verify the energy-use figures in a company's sustainability report. Which approach best applies normal audit practice?
Accept the figures because senior management approved the report
Trace sampled figures to meter readings and bills
Interview the report's author and record her answers as proof
Compare this year's totals only with last year's published totals

Sustainability claims are verified the same way as other audit data, by sampling and tracing reported figures to source records. An approval or an interview alone is not objective evidence that the numbers are correct.
std
I.A.4
Which purpose is shared by quality, environmental, safety and financial audits?
Releasing finished product for shipment to the customer
Judging conformity to criteria based on evidence
Setting penalties for any regulatory violations found
Designing the controls the auditee should put in place

All of these audits compare objective evidence with defined criteria to reach conclusions. Releasing product and designing controls are management responsibilities, and doing them would compromise the auditor's independence.
std
I.A.4
An internal audit group carries out both financial and quality audits. Which practice applies equally to both?
Giving an opinion on whether financial statements are fairly stated
Checking the calibration status of measuring equipment in use
Drawing conclusions from verifiable evidence taken from samples
Reconciling account balances in the general ledger each month
Basing conclusions on sampled, verifiable evidence is common to every type of audit. The other options belong to one discipline only, or are routine accounting work rather than auditing.
std
I.A.4
A quality auditor is assigned to audit a plant's compliance with its environmental permit. What should she do first?
Use her usual ISO 9001 checklist so that results can be compared
Ask an environmental engineer to carry out the interviews for her
Limit the audit to records, since the processes are not quality ones
Learn the permit's conditions, since they become the audit criteria
The methods of auditing carry over, but the criteria change, so she must understand the permit's requirements before planning. A quality checklist would compare evidence against the wrong criteria.
std
I.B.1
An audit's purpose is to verify that the corrective action for a labeling error on line 3 is working. Which scope fits that purpose best?
All QMS processes at the site against every ISO 9001 clause
Every packaging line at all of the company's plants
Line 3's output and cost results for the past full year
Labeling on line 3 and its records since the fix was made

Scope should follow from purpose: verifying one corrective action calls for a narrow scope covering the affected activity and the period since the change. A full system scope spends effort far beyond what the purpose requires.
std
I.B.1
Which item belongs in an audit's scope statement rather than in its objective?
The locations, processes and time period to be covered
The reason the audit is being carried out at all
The conclusion that the client expects the audit to reach
The corrective actions that the auditee must complete
Scope defines the extent and boundaries of the audit, such as sites, processes and dates. The reason for the audit is the objective, which drives the scope but is stated separately.
std
I.B.1
Which is the best-written audit objective?
Look into calibration and find whatever problems exist
Audit the calibration lab on May 4 from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m.
Make the calibration technicians follow procedures
Determine whether calibration conforms to procedure CP-12

A good objective states what the audit will determine and against which criterion. The time slot describes the schedule and scope, and the others are vague or describe management action rather than an audit result.
std
I.B.1
A planned audit's purpose changes from verifying one corrective action at a supplier to deciding whether to approve that supplier for a new product line. How should the scope change?
Keep it the same, since the auditee and site have not changed
Widen it to the supplier's processes that affect the new product
Narrow it to the records of the original corrective action
Limit it to a desk review of the supplier's quality manual

A supplier approval decision needs evidence on every process that affects the new product, so the scope must widen to match the new purpose. Keeping the old scope would leave most of the needed evidence uncollected.
std
I.B.1
A certification body's purpose is to decide whether to certify the QMS for an entire site. The auditee asks to leave the warehouse out because it is not quality-related. What is the best response?
Leave it out, because the auditee alone decides what the audit covers
Leave it out and audit it later through a separate desk review
Leave it out unless a customer has complained about shipping
Keep it in, since storage and handling affect product conformity

When the purpose is certification of the whole site's QMS, activities that affect conformity, such as preservation and handling, belong in scope. Scope is agreed with the client and the certification body; the auditee cannot simply remove an area that the purpose requires.
std
I.B.2
Why do senior managers value audits in addition to the reports each department sends about its own performance?
Audits replace the need for departments to measure their own work
Audit reports are written in more detail than department reports
Auditors set the targets that each department is measured against
Auditors independent of the work give a more objective view of it
An audit's main value is an independent, evidence-based assessment that does not depend on the people doing the work. It complements department measurement rather than replacing it.
std
I.B.2
An audit finds every procedure step followed, yet the process misses its yield target every month. What does this tell management?
The process is effective, because every procedure step is followed
The process is efficient but does not comply with its procedure
The audit criteria must be wrong, because the process conforms
The process conforms but is not effective at achieving its results
Effectiveness is the extent to which planned results are achieved, so a conforming process that misses its target is not effective. Following the procedure shows conformity, not effectiveness.
std
I.B.2
An audit finds a purchase approval loop with five signatures that adds nine days but has never caught an error. This observation mainly concerns:
Effectiveness
Conformity
Legal compliance
Efficiency

Efficiency is the relationship between results and the resources used, and five signatures that add delay but no value are waste. The process still achieves its result, so effectiveness is not the main issue.
std
I.B.2
An audit of the warranty process finds that claims are paid without anyone confirming that the product failed. What is the main benefit of this finding to management?
It proves that the product design itself is defective
It exposes a financial risk management can control
It shows that customers are filing false warranty claims
It confirms that the warranty terms are too generous

Paying unverified claims is a control gap that exposes the company to financial loss, and the audit brings it to management's attention. The finding does not by itself prove fraud or design defects; it shows the control is missing.
std
I.B.2
An audit of a supplier finds customer drawings on a shared drive that every user, including temporary staff, can open, and no access logs are kept. Which risk does this mainly reveal?
Information security
Product conformity
Environmental compliance
Workplace safety

Uncontrolled access to customer technical data with no logging is an information security weakness that audits can expose. It does not show that any product fails requirements, so product conformity is not the main risk.
std
I.B.2
A plant manager wants audits to add value beyond a pass or fail on the standard. Which use of audit results does that best?
Counting how many audits were completed against the schedule
Linking findings to scrap cost, delivery and complaint trends
Ranking auditors by the number of findings each one writes
Posting the number of nonconformities found per department

Relating audit results to business measures such as cost, delivery and customer complaints helps management see where the system affects performance. Counting audits or findings measures audit activity, not organizational results.
std
I.B.2
Management points to low nonconformity counts from audits that process owners carried out on their own areas as proof that the system is effective. What is the main weakness of this evidence?
The audits produced too few findings to calculate useful statistics
The audits were internal, and only external audits show effectiveness
The audits lacked independence, so the results may not be objective
The audits checked conformity, which can never show effectiveness
People auditing their own work may not see or report their own problems, so the low counts are weak evidence. Internal audits can show effectiveness when auditors are independent of the area audited.
std
I.C
A supplier is audited against ISO 9001. How is this audit criterion best classified?
An industry-specific standard
An international standard
A national regulation
An internal policy

ISO 9001 is published by the International Organization for Standardization and applies across industries and countries. It is not a regulation, because it is voluntary unless a contract or law makes it a requirement.
std
I.C
A supplier of aircraft parts is audited against a sector QMS standard that adds aerospace requirements to the ISO 9001 base. How is this criterion best classified?
A national regulation
A customer specification
An industry standard
An internal procedure

A standard written for one sector, adding that industry's requirements to a general base, is an industry standard. It is not a customer specification, because it applies across the whole sector rather than to one buyer's parts.
std
I.C
A supplier's contract requires it to conform to a standard published by its country's national standards body. Which statement is true?
It is binding on every company in that country by national law
It overrides the contract wherever the two disagree
It is a national standard, made binding here by the contract
It applies only once it is adopted as an ISO standard
National standards are generally voluntary; here the contract makes this one a requirement for the supplier. A standard does not become law for everyone just because a national body publishes it.
std
I.C
In a second-party audit, a supplier samples one part in ten for pressure testing as its procedure says, but the purchase contract requires every part to be tested. Which criterion governs?
The supplier's own sampling procedure
The contract's requirement to test every part
The auditor's judgment of what is reasonable
The ISO 9001 clause on monitoring and measurement

The contract is the agreed customer requirement, and a supplier procedure that conflicts with it does not override it. ISO 9001 does not set test frequencies; it requires the organization to meet customer requirements.
std
I.C
A contract manufacturer and its client sign a document defining who approves changes, who releases lots and how deviations must be reported. What is this document?
A product specification
A quality agreement
A purchase order
An audit plan

A quality agreement sets out the quality responsibilities of each party and is a valid audit criterion. A specification defines product or process characteristics, not who is responsible for which quality tasks.
std
I.C
An auditor finds a part measured at 10.08 mm against a drawing requirement of 10.00 ± 0.05 mm. Which criterion was not met?
The quality policy
The international standard
The quality agreement
The product specification
The drawing dimension and tolerance are a specification, and 10.08 mm is above the 10.05 mm upper limit. The international standard does not define the part's dimensions.
std
I.C
A company's quality policy commits to answering every customer complaint within two business days. An internal auditor finds complaints answered in eight days on average. Can this support a finding?
No, only external standards and contracts can serve as audit criteria
No, a policy states intent and so cannot be audited
Yes, the policy is a valid internal criterion for the audit
Only if the customer contract repeats the commitment

Audit criteria include the organization's own policies and commitments, so a measurable policy statement can be audited. Limiting criteria to external standards would leave most internal requirements unaudited.
std
I.C
In a first-party audit of a process, which source usually gives the most detailed criteria?
The international QMS standard it is certified to
The national standards body's published guidance
The company's own procedures and work instructions
The certificate issued by the certification body

Internal QMS documents describe how each process is meant to run in detail, so they are the main criteria for a process audit. The international standard sets general requirements but does not describe the company's specific methods.
std
I.C
A company's internal procedure is stricter than ISO 9001 requires, and the auditor finds it is not being followed, though the standard's own minimum is met. What should the auditor do?
Record no finding, since the standard is still met
Recommend lowering the procedure to the standard
Report a nonconformity against the internal procedure
Report it only as an opportunity for improvement

The organization's own documented arrangements are audit criteria, and failing to follow them is a nonconformity even if a looser external requirement is met. Treating it only as an improvement opportunity ignores the requirement the company set for itself.
std
I.D
Who is responsible for directing the audit team and for the final content of the audit report?
The client
The auditee's representative
The lead auditor
The observer
The lead auditor manages the team, makes final decisions on findings and is responsible for the report. The client requests the audit and receives the report but does not decide its content.
std
I.D
A purchasing director asks the supplier quality group to audit a new supplier and will use the report to decide whether to approve it. In this audit, what is her role?
Client
Auditee
Lead auditor
Observer
The client is the person or organization that requests the audit and uses its results. The auditee is the supplier being audited.
std
I.D
Which of these is a responsibility of the auditee?
Giving access to the areas, people and records needed
Deciding which of the findings the auditors are allowed to report
Selecting the members of the audit team on the client's behalf
Approving the audit conclusions before the closing meeting

The auditee's main duties are to cooperate, provide access and resources, and act on the results. Selecting the team and deciding on findings belong to the client, the program manager and the lead auditor.
std
I.D
A regulator's representative goes along with an audit team as an observer and begins questioning operators about their work. What should the lead auditor do?
Remind him that observers do not take part in the audit
Record the operators' answers to his questions as evidence
Hand him part of the checklist so that he can help the team
Ask the auditee whether it minds the extra questions

Observers may accompany the team but should not take part in or interfere with the audit, and the lead auditor controls this. Using his questions as evidence would treat him as an auditor, which he is not.
std
I.D
While auditing receiving, an audit team member notices a possible problem in an area assigned to another team member. What should she do?
Ignore it, since the area is outside her assignment
Write it up herself as a major nonconformity
Tell the operator in that area to fix it right away
Tell the lead auditor, who decides how it is handled

Team members work within their assignments and pass information outside them to the lead auditor, who coordinates the team. Ignoring it could lose evidence, and telling the operator to fix it goes beyond an auditor's role.
std
I.D
A team auditing a sterilization process adds a specialist who explains validation methods to the auditors but does not act as an auditor. What is the specialist's role?
Technical expert
Observer
Guide
Auditor-in-training
A technical expert gives the team specific knowledge or expertise but does not act as an auditor. An observer only accompanies the team and gives no expertise to it.
std
I.D
Who is appointed by the auditee to escort the audit team, arrange access to people and areas, and make sure site safety rules are followed?
The observer
The technical expert
The guide
The client
A guide (escort) is named by the auditee to help the team with access, contacts and safety. An observer accompanies the team but has no duty to assist it.
std
I.D

After the closing meeting, the client asks the lead auditor to drop a finding from the report because it might harm the supplier relationship. The finding is supported by objective evidence. What should the lead auditor do?
Remove it, since the audit report belongs to the client
Move it into a separate memo kept off the record
Keep the finding, since it is supported by evidence
Downgrade it to a verbal comment given privately

The lead auditor is responsible for an accurate report, and evidence-based findings should not be removed for business convenience. The client receives and controls distribution of the report but does not decide which supported findings it contains.
std
I.E.1
A supplier's quality manager offers an auditor expensive tickets to a sports event as thanks during the audit. What should the auditor do?
Decline politely, since it could appear to sway his judgment
Accept, as long as the audit report has already been sent
Accept and mention the gift in the audit report
Accept, since refusing could harm the supplier working relationship

The spirit of the ASQ Code of Ethics is to avoid anything that could compromise or appear to compromise professional judgment. Disclosing the gift does not remove the appearance of influence, so declining is the right choice.
std
I.E.1
An auditor is assigned to audit a process that relies on technology she has never worked with. What does ethical practice call for?
Audit it anyway and rely on the auditee's explanations of the technology
Limit the audit to records so the gap is not noticed
Disclose the gap and ask for a technical expert or reassignment
Turn down the assignment without giving a reason

Professionals should take on only work they are competent to do, or get the support they need, and be honest about their limits. Hiding the gap behind a records-only audit would mislead the client about what was examined.
std
I.E.1
An audit team plans to accept a supplier's certificates of conformance for a critical alloy without checking anything behind them. What does due diligence call for?
Verifying a sample of the test data behind the certificates
Accepting the certificates, since the supplier signed them
Asking the supplier to sign a second declaration
Rejecting the certificates and requiring full retesting

Due diligence means taking reasonable steps to verify information before relying on it, such as checking a sample of the underlying results. Rejecting everything and requiring full retesting goes beyond what is reasonable without evidence of a problem.
std
I.E.1
For an auditor, due care means:
Guaranteeing that no nonconformity goes undetected
Using the skill and caution a prudent auditor would use
Checking every record instead of taking samples
Deferring to the auditee's experts on technical questions
Due care is the standard of a reasonably careful, competent professional in the same situation. It does not require perfection or 100% checking, since audits rely on sampling.
std
I.E.1
During an audit of one supplier, the quality manager asks the auditor how a competing supplier she audited last month solved a similar problem. What should she do?
Share it, as long as the competitor is not named
Share it, since it would help improve quality
Refer him to the competitor's quality manager
Decline to share what she learned in the other audit

Information obtained during an audit is confidential and must not be passed to others, especially competitors. Leaving out the name does not make it acceptable, because the information still belongs to the other supplier.
std
I.E.1
An auditor is assigned to audit a supplier where her brother is the plant manager. What should she do?
Accept and take extra care to be objective
Accept, but not interview her brother
Accept, since the audit is of the system, not people
Disclose the relationship and ask to be reassigned

A close family relationship is a conflict of interest that must be disclosed, and reassignment protects the audit's credibility. Trying hard to be objective does not remove the conflict or how it looks to others.
std
I.E.1
During an audit, an auditor finds clear evidence that test results were altered so that failing lots could ship. What should she do?
Record the facts and report them promptly to the client
Confront the technician and demand an explanation
Leave it out, since fraud is outside the audit scope
Ask the auditee to fix the records before the report

Possible illegal activity should be documented factually and reported promptly through the agreed channel, normally to the lead auditor and client. Confronting the person is not the auditor's role and could compromise any later investigation.
std
I.E.1
During a plant tour, an auditor sees a worker reach inside a running press with its guard interlock bypassed. What should she do?
Note it and raise it as a finding at the closing meeting
Take a photo for the report and continue with the tour
Say nothing, since safety is outside the audit scope
Alert the guide or supervisor at once so the danger is stopped

An imminent danger to people must be reported immediately so it can be stopped, whatever the audit's scope. Waiting until the closing meeting leaves the worker exposed to serious injury in the meantime.
std
I.E.1
An auditor notices a blocked fire exit in an area outside the audit scope; no one is in immediate danger. What is the most appropriate action?
Tell auditee management promptly, though it is out of scope
Ignore it, since only areas in scope may be reported on
Write it up as a major nonconformity in the audit report
Call the local fire authority before telling anyone on site

Unsafe conditions should be brought to the auditee's attention promptly, even when they are outside scope, so they can be corrected. Writing it up as a nonconformity is not right, because the area was not part of the audit.
std
I.E.2

To finish early, a certification auditor skips the planned review of a supplier's critical heat-treat records. The supplier later ships parts that fail in service from that process. What is a possible consequence?
None, since the supplier alone is responsible for what it ships
The auditor becomes liable for every part the supplier ships
The customer's warranty duties pass to the certification body
The certification body may face negligence claims

Skipping planned work without justification falls short of due care and can expose the auditor and the certification body to claims and loss of trust. The supplier remains responsible for its product, but that does not erase the auditor's own exposure.
std
I.E.2
An internal audit report records a missing machine guard. Management does not act, and a worker is later injured on that machine. How may the audit report affect the company?
It protects the company, since the hazard was found by its audit
It moves legal responsibility for the injury onto the auditor
It can show the company knew and did not act
It has no effect, since internal reports are always private
Audit records can show that the organization knew about a problem and did not correct it, which increases its liability. Finding a hazard protects no one unless it is acted on.
std
I.E.2
Which statement is best for an audit report, considering possible legal use of the record?
The operators seem careless and the product may be unsafe
Testing is a disaster and should be shut down at once
Two of five sampled test records lacked operator sign-off
Records are poor, as everyone in the plant already knows

Reports should state verifiable facts tied to evidence. Opinions and speculation, such as calling operators careless or product unsafe, are not supported and can create legal exposure for both the auditor and the auditee.
std
I.E.2
A supplier auditor carelessly approves a supplier that cannot hold a critical tolerance. What is the most direct financial impact on the buying company?
Costs of scrap, rework, containment and possibly recalls
Higher fees for its next certification audit
Lower wages for the supplier quality auditors
A smaller budget for its internal audit program next year
An approval based on careless auditing lets nonconforming product into the supply chain, which drives failure costs. The other options are not direct results of the approval error.
std
I.E.2
Why should audit records be accurate, factual and kept only as long as policy requires?
They can be requested as evidence in legal proceedings
Auditees may rewrite them once the audit is closed
They are the main source of the auditor's own pay
Certification bodies destroy any records they review
Audit records may be sought in disputes or lawsuits, so they must be accurate and handled according to retention policy. Auditees do not have the right to rewrite audit records.
std
I.E.2
Which situation best describes negligence by an auditor?
Finding no nonconformities after following the full audit plan
Skipping a required calibration check on a critical gauge
Using a sample rather than checking every single record
Reporting a finding that the auditee strongly disagrees with

Negligence is failing to do what a reasonably careful auditor would do, such as skipping a required check on a critical item. Sampling is accepted practice, and finding nothing after a proper audit is not a failure of care.
std
I.E.3
Which assignment best protects independence in an internal audit of purchasing?
The purchasing supervisor, who knows the process in detail
The buyer who wrote the current purchasing procedure
A trained engineer with no purchasing duties
The purchasing manager's assistant, who handles the files
Auditors should not audit their own work or work they report into. Detailed process knowledge is helpful, but the supervisor and the procedure's author are too close to the work to be independent.
std
I.E.3
An auditor had a bad experience with an auditee's quality manager at a former job and already believes the site is sloppy. What best protects objectivity?
Keep the history private and write fewer findings to stay balanced
Look harder for problems, since she expects to find them anyway
Ask the quality manager to agree to each finding before it is written
Disclose the history and base conclusions only on evidence
Disclosing a possible bias and grounding every conclusion in evidence protect objectivity. Writing fewer findings to compensate is also biased, just in the other direction.
std
I.E.3
Which auditor behavior most undermines objectivity?
Using a checklist prepared during planning
Taking a random sample of records to review
Settling on findings before collecting evidence
Confirming a fact through a second source
Objectivity means letting the evidence decide the conclusions. Deciding the findings in advance reverses that. Checklists, random samples and corroboration all support objective auditing.
std
I.E.3
A customer questions an audit's conclusions about a supplier's welding process. Which fact most strengthens the audit's credibility?
The audit was carried out in less time than was planned
The supplier agreed with all of the conclusions in advance
The auditor had audited the supplier many times before
The auditor was qualified in auditing and in welding

Qualifications in both audit methods and the technical subject show the auditor could judge the evidence soundly. Repeated visits to the same supplier can actually reduce independence rather than build credibility.
std
I.E.3
A small company has one trained internal auditor, the quality manager, who also runs the QMS. How can it best keep its internal audits credible?
Let her audit everything, since she knows the system best
Bring in a qualified outsider for her processes
Skip auditing the QMS processes she is responsible for
Have the production staff audit her processes untrained

Using a qualified outsider for the processes she runs keeps the auditor independent of the work while keeping competence. Untrained staff would be independent but not qualified, which also weakens credibility.
std
II.A.1
A plant manager asks a quality engineer to audit the purchasing department of a sister division that reports to a different vice president. What should the engineer do before planning anything else?
Ask the plant manager which problems he expects the audit to find
Confirm who authorized the audit and that it covers that division
Draft a checklist from the purchasing procedure and ISO 9001
Contact the purchasing manager to agree on convenient audit dates

An audit needs a client with the authority to commission it over the area audited; without that, the auditee can refuse and the results carry no weight. Agreeing dates or drafting a checklist comes after authority is settled.
std
II.A.1
A customer asks a supplier to audit only the heat-treat process linked to last quarter's field failures. How should this purpose shape the scope?
Cover the final inspection records for the parts already shipped
Cover every process at the site that makes the customer's parts
Cover heat treatment with its direct inputs, controls and records
Cover every ISO 9001 clause so no systemic cause can be missed

Scope follows purpose: a focused purpose calls for a scope drawn around the process in question and what feeds it. Auditing every clause or every process dilutes the effort, and final inspection alone cannot show why heat treatment failed.
std
II.A.1
Management wants to know whether one product family meets all its drawing and packaging requirements as it is ready to ship. Which audit type fits this purpose best?
System audit of the QMS
Compliance audit of the QMS
Management audit
Product audit

A product audit examines finished product against its specified requirements, which is exactly the question asked. A system audit looks at whether the management system as a whole is in place and effective, not at a specific product's conformance.
std
II.A.1
A supplier audit is due next month. Only one auditor can travel, most records are electronic, and a key operation is manual welding. Which format suits this best?
A desk audit of the welding procedure and welder qualification records
Hybrid, with records reviewed remotely and one auditor on-site to watch welding
Fully on-site, delaying the audit until the whole team can travel
Fully remote, using welding video the supplier records in advance

A hybrid format uses remote review where records are electronic and puts a person where live observation matters. Prerecorded video is chosen and staged by the auditee, so it is weak evidence of normal practice.
std
II.A.1
While planning a remote audit, what should the lead auditor confirm with the auditee?
That written answers will replace live interviews
That no live views of work areas will be requested
That all records will be emailed to the team before the audit begins
That the video tools work and sensitive files can be shared securely

Remote audits depend on reliable technology and on secure handling of the auditee's information, so both are settled in planning. Sending everything in advance or replacing interviews with written answers removes the live sampling and questioning that make audit evidence credible.
std
II.A.1
A lead auditor is planning an internal audit of a molding area that supplies automotive customers. Which set of criteria is most complete?
ISO 9001 and the quality manual, since customers check their own needs
The molding work instructions, since this is a process audit
ISO 9001, customer-specific requirements, regulations and internal procedures
The previous audit report and the latest customer scorecard

Criteria are the full set of requirements the area must meet, which for an automotive supplier includes customer-specific requirements and any applicable laws as well as the standard and internal procedures. Leaving customer requirements to the customer misses obligations the site has accepted.
std
II.A.1
While planning an audit of a plating line, the lead auditor learns that wastewater discharge is covered by a government permit. The audit's purpose includes regulatory compliance. What should she do?
Leave the permit out, since quality audits address customer requirements
Add the permit conditions to the audit criteria
Ask the plating supervisor to certify compliance in writing at the opening
Mention the permit in the report as an opportunity for improvement

When the purpose includes regulatory compliance, the applicable legal requirements become audit criteria. A supervisor's written assurance is not audit evidence, and an improvement note does not test compliance at all.
std
II.A.1
While planning a process audit of order entry, an auditor sketches the process with its inputs, outputs and the departments it hands work to. What is the main value of this step?
It removes the need to interview people in order entry
It shows interfaces and where the scope starts and ends
It provides the procedure that order entry has not written
It lets the auditor draft findings before arriving on site

Mapping a process exposes hand-offs, where many failures occur, and makes the audit boundaries explicit. A map is a planning aid for the auditor; it does not replace interviews or become the auditee's procedure.
std
II.A.1

A process map shows that engineering changes are released by design engineering but put into effect on the floor by production planning. For an audit of change control, what does this tell the auditor?
The audit must include the hand-off between the two departments
The audit should become two separate audits with no shared plan
The audit can focus on design engineering, which owns the change
The audit can focus on production planning, which does the work

Change control crosses a department boundary, and the hand-off is where changes are most likely to be lost or delayed, so it must be in scope. Auditing either side alone cannot show that a released change actually reaches the floor.
std
II.A.1
A planned two-day audit covers three shifts and a sterilization process that no team member understands. What is the best adjustment to resources?
Keep the team as it is and rely on the checklist for technical content
Ask the sterilization supervisor to audit that area for the team
Add a technical expert and plan coverage of the off shifts
Limit the audit to day shift and drop sterilization from scope

Resources must match the scope: technical gaps are filled with an expert, and time is planned so every shift in scope is seen. Using the area's own supervisor breaks independence, and quietly cutting scope defeats the audit's purpose.
std
II.A.1
A corporate audit covers four plants in one week with a fixed set of criteria. Which planning decision fits best?
Form several teams, each led on site, under one coordinating lead auditor
Have each plant audit itself and send its own results to the lead auditor
Send one auditor to each plant, each working from a personal checklist
Use one team that spends a few hours at each of the four plants

Large multi-site scopes call for more than one team, with coordination so all teams apply the same criteria and methods. Self-audits by each plant lose independence, and separate personal checklists make results inconsistent.
std
II.A.1
During planning, the lead auditor and the client agree on the report format, who receives copies and how long audit records are kept. Which planning element does this address?
Criteria the audit will be judged against
Authority under which the audit is held
Scope of the audit and its boundaries
Documentation requirements

Report format, distribution and record retention are documentation requirements set during planning. Scope defines the extent of the audit and criteria define what it is measured against; neither covers how results are recorded and kept.
std
II.A.2

Two employees are considered for an internal QMS audit. One has an engineering degree and no audit training. The other has ten years in production, auditor training and three supervised audits. Who is better suited to audit now?
Neither, since internal audits need an outside certified auditor
The engineer, since formal education outweighs practical experience
The production employee, who has audit training and supervised practice
Either, since availability is the main factor in auditor selection

Auditor competence combines education with audit training and practice, and supervised audits are direct evidence of the needed skill. A degree alone does not show the ability to plan, sample and judge evidence.
std
II.A.2
When choosing a lead auditor for a complex audit of several sites, which factor matters most beyond basic auditor training?
Seniority and rank in the company's management structure
Experience leading teams on audits of similar scope
Personal familiarity with the auditee's managers
A large number of years since completing training

Leading a complex audit requires experience directing teams, managing schedules and resolving conflicts, which comes from having done it. Rank and personal ties do not show that skill, and personal ties can harm objectivity.
std
II.A.2
A certification body is assigning auditors for a medical device maker. Why should at least one team member have a medical device background?
To let the team give the auditee advice on product design
To shorten the audit by skipping explanations of the process
To remove the need for a lead auditor with system skills
To judge evidence against sector risks and regulations

Industry background helps the team recognize what matters in that sector and understand regulatory expectations when weighing evidence. Giving design advice would compromise the team's independence, and sector knowledge does not replace audit leadership.
std
II.A.2
An audit of a nondestructive testing lab requires someone who can judge radiographic film quality, and no auditor has that skill. What should the lead auditor do?
Ask the lab's own senior inspector to evaluate the film for the team
Have the most senior auditor judge the film from a reference book
Add a qualified technical expert who works under an auditor's direction
Drop film interpretation from the scope without telling the client

A technical expert supplies specific knowledge the team lacks and supports, but does not act as, an auditor. The lab's own inspector is not independent of the work under review, and changing scope without the client defeats the audit.
std
II.A.2
A quality engineer wrote the calibration procedure last year and still maintains the calibration database. She is asked to audit calibration. What is the main concern?
She is not independent of the activity she would audit
She may lack the technical knowledge to audit calibration
Her familiarity will make the audit run longer than planned
She has not read the procedure from an auditor's viewpoint
Auditors should not audit their own work, because they are unlikely to see its weaknesses objectively. Her technical knowledge is a strength; the problem is that she is part of the activity.
std
II.A.2
A small company has three trained internal auditors, all in the quality department. The quality department's own processes are due for audit. What best preserves independence?
Use a trained auditor from another function or from outside
Have the quality manager review his own department's records
Skip the quality department, since it audits everyone else
Let each quality auditor review the work she did personally

Independence means the auditor has no responsibility for the work audited, so someone outside the quality department is needed. Skipping the area leaves part of the system unaudited, and self-review is not an audit.
std
II.A.3
An auditor is preparing for a first audit of a new supplier. Which source gives the best pre-audit picture of how the supplier actually performs?
The supplier's quality policy and the date it was last approved
Incoming inspection data and complaint records for that supplier
The supplier's marketing brochure and public website
The supplier's organization chart and staff directory

Performance data from receiving and complaints shows where the supplier has actually had problems, so the audit can focus there. Policies, charts and brochures describe intent and structure, not results.
std
II.A.3
An auditor is preparing for the first audit of a newly launched internal process, which has no audit history. Where should she look first for pre-audit information?
The annual budget for the department that owns the process
Opinions about the process from employees in other areas
Its procedures, performance data and recent nonconformance reports
Audit reports from unrelated processes at the company's other sites

Process documents tell the auditor what should happen and performance and nonconformance data show where it may not, which together shape the checklist and sampling. Opinions from outside the process are hearsay, not a planning basis.
std
II.A.3
In a document review before the audit, an auditor sees that the auditee's procedure cites an older revision of the customer's specification. What should she do?
Note it and plan to check which revision is used in practice
Raise a major nonconformity before the audit begins
Ignore it, since the procedure is not the audit criterion
Cancel the audit until the procedure has been revised and reissued

Document review flags possible problems to verify on site; a finding needs evidence of what actually happens. Ignoring it misses a likely gap, since conformity to the current customer specification is part of the criteria.
std
II.A.3
Why does an auditor confirm the edition of each standard and specification listed as audit criteria during preparation?
Requirements change between editions; findings must cite the one in force
Older editions tend to be stricter and so produce more findings for the report
The auditee must buy each edition before the audit is allowed to start
The report must list the publication date of each document it cites

Clauses are added, removed and renumbered between editions, so a finding against the wrong edition may be invalid. Strictness of older editions is not the issue; using the edition the auditee is actually bound by is.
std
II.A.3
A company preparing for first certification did a gap assessment three months ago. How should the lead auditor of the internal readiness audit use it?
Focus on the gaps it found and check whether they were closed
Treat every gap it found as an open nonconformity in the new report
Set it aside, as a gap assessment is not an audit
Reuse its results as the readiness audit's findings

A gap assessment shows where the organization fell short of requirements, so the readiness audit should test whether those gaps have since been addressed. Old results are not current evidence, so they cannot simply become today's findings.
std
II.A.3
What best describes a gap assessment?
A review limited to financial controls and the costs of poor quality
A certification audit performed on site by a third-party registrar
A comparison of practice against requirements to find what is missing
An audit that ends in formal corrective action requests to the auditee

A gap assessment measures the distance between what an organization does and what a standard or customer requires, usually to plan implementation. It is a planning tool rather than a conformity audit, so it does not normally issue formal corrective action requests.
std
II.A.3
The prior audit of shipping found repeated labeling errors, and the corrective action was closed two months ago. How should this affect planning for the next shipping audit?
Assign the same auditor again so the approach is consistent
Exclude labeling, since the corrective action is already closed
Copy the prior checklist exactly so results can be compared
Include a check that the labeling action is working
Prior audit results point to areas of risk, and a recently closed action needs evidence that it is effective over time. Closure on paper does not show the problem stopped recurring.
std
II.A.4
An audit includes a pharmaceutical clean room and an area with industrial lasers. What logistics step matters most?
Learn the entry, gowning and safety rules for each area beforehand
Plan to photograph conditions in each area to include in the report
Ask that the lasers be shut down for the entire audit
Plan to skip both areas if the schedule runs short

Auditors must be able to enter hazardous or controlled areas safely and without contaminating them, which requires learning the rules in advance. Shutting down equipment stops the auditor from seeing normal operation.
std
II.A.4
A defense contractor restricts visitors from some areas and needs advance approval for certain visitors. When should the lead auditor deal with this?
On arrival at the gate, by showing photo identification to security
During planning, by sending team details for clearance in advance
At the opening meeting, when access lists are reviewed
After the audit, as a lessons-learned item in the report
Security clearances take time, so they must be arranged in planning or auditors may be refused entry. Raising it at the opening meeting is too late to obtain approval.
std
II.A.4
Why might an auditee assign an escort to an external audit team?
To answer questions on behalf of the employees
To approve in advance the questions auditors are allowed to ask
To contest each finding as soon as it is raised
To guide the team, enforce safety rules and arrange access

Escorts or guides help the team move safely, reach the right people and areas, and observe on the auditee's behalf. Screening or answering questions for employees interferes with the audit and weakens the evidence.
std
II.A.4
A second-party auditor will review a supplier's proprietary process parameters. What should be arranged before the visit?
A confidentiality agreement covering what the auditor will see
A purchase order covering the cost of the audit
A written promise that no findings will be raised
Copies of the parameters sent to the auditor's office ahead of time
A confidentiality agreement protects the auditee's proprietary information and makes access possible. Sending the parameters off site increases exposure rather than protecting it.
std
II.A.4
On audit day, a manager refuses entry to the tool room, saying it holds trade secrets, although tooling is in the agreed scope. What planning step would most likely have prevented this?
Confirming in writing that auditors may access every area in scope
Inviting the tool room supervisor to the closing meeting
Sending the audit checklist to the tool room supervisor well in advance
Choosing an auditor with long experience in tooling
Right of access should be agreed with the client and auditee before the audit, including any limits on sensitive areas. A checklist or a skilled auditor does not settle whether the auditor may enter.
std
II.A.4
During an audit, the team is refused access to a records room that is within scope. What should the lead auditor do?
Stop the audit at once and leave the site
Raise it with the client and auditee and record the scope limitation
Skip the room and leave the matter out of the report
Write a major nonconformity against the area for refusing access to it

Obstacles to access are reported to the client and auditee so they can decide what to do, and any limitation is recorded so the conclusions are not overstated. Refusal of access is not itself evidence that the records are nonconforming.
std
II.A.4
For a three-day on-site audit, which request to the auditee is a facility accommodation?
A private room with internet access for the team
Approval of the audit criteria by the auditee's manager
An escort assigned to every auditor in the office areas
A list of nonconformities from recent internal audits
A workspace with internet lets the team meet privately, review notes and work with electronic records. The other requests concern pre-audit information, criteria and escorts rather than facilities.
std
II.A.4
A team will audit a foundry floor. How should personal protective equipment be handled?
Let each auditor decide on arrival what protective equipment seems needed
Avoid the floor and review the foundry's records only
Confirm PPE needs in planning so the team brings or is issued it
Have the escort lend his own PPE to auditors as needed
PPE requirements are a logistics item settled before the visit so auditors can enter safely and on time. Avoiding the floor gives up direct observation of the process being audited.
std
II.A.5
An auditor must check 600 completed work orders for operator sign-off and has time for about 30. Which approach gives the most defensible result?
Review the first 30 work orders of the audit period
Pick a random sample spread across shifts and the audit period
Review the 30 most recent work orders in the file
Ask the area supervisor to pick 30 typical work orders for review
