A random sample spread across the population gives every record a chance of selection and avoids bias toward one time or shift. Letting the auditee choose the sample invites selection of good records.
std
II.A.5
An auditor decides to sample more heavily from a new production line that had start-up problems. What kind of sampling is this?
Lot-by-lot acceptance sampling
Systematic sampling at fixed intervals
Judgment-based sampling
Simple random sampling of all lines
Choosing where to sample from knowledge of risk is judgment-based sampling. Random and systematic samples are drawn without regard to where problems are expected.
std
II.A.5
What is a limitation of judgment-based audit sampling compared with statistical sampling?
It is not permitted under ISO 19011 audit guidance
It cannot be aimed at the areas of highest risk in the scope
Its results cannot be projected statistically to the population
It needs a larger sample than statistical methods do to be valid

Judgment-based samples are chosen by the auditor, so no confidence level can be attached to conclusions about the whole population. Targeting high-risk areas is the method's strength, not a limitation.
std
II.A.5
An audit program procedure requires every audit to use the same finding grades, sampling approach and way of recording evidence. What is the main benefit?
Fewer findings are raised, so corrective action drops
Results are consistent and comparable across auditors and audits
Each auditor is free to choose the method that suits her personal style
Audits are shorter because no further planning is needed
Common procedural guidelines mean that a finding means the same thing whoever wrote it, so results can be compared and trended. Standard methods support planning; they do not remove it.
std
II.A.5
What is a key risk of using a checklist during an audit?
It stops the auditee from preparing properly for the audit visit
The auditor may follow it rigidly and miss evidence outside it
It cannot be kept as a record of the audit
It must be approved by the registrar before use
Checklists keep an audit on track but can narrow attention, so auditors should follow up on what they see even when it is not on the list. A completed checklist is a useful record of the audit.
std
II.A.5
An auditor is writing a checklist for an audit of calibration. Which item is best written?
Ask the technician about any calibration problems he has had lately
Is there a documented calibration procedure? Answer yes or no
Is calibration of measuring equipment performed at this site?
Check calibration status and traceability of five gauges in use
A good checklist item names what to sample and what to verify, which produces objective evidence. Yes-or-no questions about whether something exists say nothing about whether it is done correctly.
std
II.A.5
During an audit, what is a log sheet mainly used for?
Scheduling interviews with each department
Summarizing the findings and conclusions for the final audit report
Listing the questions to ask in each area
Recording items sampled, such as record numbers and dates
A log sheet captures the trail of what was examined so the sample can be traced and repeated. The questions to ask belong on the checklist, and summaries belong in the report.
std
II.A.5
Which working paper is used to record a single nonconformity with the requirement and the evidence?
Opening meeting attendance sheet
Sample log sheet for the area
Audit plan with team assignments
Nonconformity report form
A nonconformity report form captures the requirement, the evidence and the statement of nonconformity in a set format. A log sheet records what was sampled but does not state a finding.
std
II.A.5
An audit team plans to record notes on tablets that sync to a cloud service. What should the lead auditor confirm first?
That any paper notes are destroyed after the audit
That auditee data stays secure and records are kept as required
That every auditor types faster than she writes
That the auditee can view and edit the team's notes during the audit
Electronic working papers must protect confidential information and meet record retention rules. Letting the auditee edit the auditor's notes would destroy their integrity.
std
II.A.5
An auditee forbids electronic devices in its production area. How should the team record evidence there?
On paper working papers prepared for that area
From memory, writing notes after leaving the area
Skip recording evidence from that area for this audit
By asking the escort to email photos of the area later

Where electronic devices are not allowed, the documentation method switches to manual records planned in advance. Notes written later from memory are less reliable, and photos chosen by the escort are not the auditor's own evidence.
std
II.A.6
An auditor picks a customer order and follows it from order entry through planning, production, inspection and shipment. Which technique is this?
Forward tracing
Discovery approach
Element-by-element audit
Backward tracing
Following work from its start in the order direction it flows is forward tracing. Backward tracing starts from an output and works toward the inputs.
std
II.A.6
An auditor wants to confirm that a special requirement on a customer order reached the work instructions and the inspection plan. Which approach fits best?
Backward tracing from a recent shipment
Discovery walk on the shop floor
Observation of the final packing area
Forward tracing from the order
Starting at the order and following the requirement downstream shows whether it was carried into each later document. Starting from a shipment could pick an order with no special requirement.
std
II.A.6
A customer reports a field failure. The auditor wants to find which materials, processes and checks the failed unit went through. Which technique fits best?
Forward tracing from a newly entered order
Observation of the work on the current shift
Discovery walk through the receiving area
Backward tracing from the failed unit

Backward tracing starts with an output, here the failed unit, and follows its records back through each step to its inputs. Forward tracing from a new order would not tell the auditor what happened to the unit that failed.
std
II.A.6
An auditor walks into the stockroom with no preset trail, notices untagged parts on the floor and follows up from there. Which technique is this?
Discovery
Forward tracing
Element-by-element audit
Backward tracing
In the discovery approach the auditor lets what is seen in the area direct the next questions. Tracing follows a set path of a product or record, which was not the case here.
std
II.A.6
What is a drawback of relying mainly on the discovery approach?
It requires the auditee to choose the samples the auditor will examine
It is limited to desk audits with no site visit
Coverage of the scope may be uneven and hard to show
It cannot find nonconformities in actual practice

Because the path is set by what the auditor happens to notice, some parts of the scope may get little attention and coverage is difficult to demonstrate. Finding real problems in practice is the approach's strength.
std
II.A.6
Records show that operators perform a torque check every hour. Which gives the strongest evidence that this happens?
Asking the supervisor whether checks are done
Seeing that the torque check form exists and has been approved
Reading the procedure that requires the check
Watching operators do the check during the shift
Direct observation of the activity shows it being done as required. A procedure or blank form shows only that the check is defined, and a supervisor's word is unverified.
std
II.A.6
Why should an auditor be cautious about relying on one observation of a task?
Observations need a measurement before they count as audit evidence
People act differently when watched, and one case may not be typical
Observation is not accepted as objective evidence in most audit types
Auditors may not watch work unless a supervisor is also present

Observation is strong evidence, but a single instance may not represent normal practice, so auditors combine it with records or further sampling. Observation itself is a recognized source of objective evidence.
std
II.A.7
A lead auditor has the scope, criteria, team and dates agreed. What else should the audit plan contain?
Who audits which areas, when, and by what methods
The deadlines for the auditee's corrective actions
The nonconformities expected in each area
The scores each area received the previous year

An audit plan assigns team members to areas, sets the schedule and states the methods, including sampling, so the audit can be carried out and coordinated. Expected nonconformities would show bias before any evidence is collected.
std
II.A.7
A lead auditor is drafting the plan for a two-day process audit. Planning showed that heat treatment had three customer complaints this year and packaging had none. How should the plan reflect this?
Leave packaging out because it had no complaints this year
Split the time equally among all areas to be fair to each
Audit heat treatment last in case the time runs short
Give heat treatment more time and a larger sample
A plan built from planning information puts effort where risk is highest. Dropping packaging changes the agreed scope; it should still be covered, just with less time.
std
II.A.7
An audit plan schedules interviews with second-shift press operators at 10:00 on day one. What is wrong?
Operators are not normally interviewed in a process audit
The plan should not name the work area being audited
The time does not match when that shift works
Interviews should not be scheduled in advance of the audit
A plan must fit the auditee's operations, including when each shift works, or the planned evidence cannot be collected. Scheduling interviews and naming areas are normal parts of a plan.
std
II.A.7
The lead auditor sends the plan to the auditee, who objects that the dates fall during a planned shutdown. What should happen?
Audit during the shutdown and record a lack of activity
Resolve the objection with the client and auditee before the audit
Keep the dates, since the client has already approved the audit plan
Let the auditee pick any date after the shutdown ends

The plan is shared so the auditee can raise objections, which are resolved with the client and auditee before on-site work begins. Auditing a shutdown would not show normal operation, and the auditee alone cannot reset the schedule.
std
II.A.7
Before an external audit begins, who should normally receive the audit plan?
The auditee's main customers and its regulators
Every employee who may be interviewed during the audit
The client, the auditee and the audit team
The audit team alone, so the audit stays unannounced

The plan goes to those who must act on it: the client who commissioned the audit, the auditee who must prepare, and the team who will carry it out. Unannounced audits are a special case, not normal practice.
std
II.A.7
An internal audit of maintenance will include contractors who work on site. Who else should receive the plan?
No one beyond the maintenance department manager
Every employee who works in the maintenance area on any shift
The contractor's site supervisor, so staff are available
The contractor's own corporate audit department
Stakeholders whose people or areas are involved need the plan so they can make staff and records available. Sending it to an unrelated audit department or every employee adds nothing.
std
II.B.1
Midway through day one, an auditor is two hours behind because one interview ran long. What is the best first step?
Work late to catch up without telling the auditee
Shorten each remaining interview to recover the time
Skip the remaining areas and record them as conforming in the report
Reprioritize the remaining work by risk with the lead auditor

When time runs short, the team decides together what matters most so the highest-risk areas are still covered. Recording unaudited areas as conforming is false, and changing hours without notice disrupts the auditee.
std
II.B.1
On day two, one auditor has finished her areas early, while another has found a pattern of problems that needs more sampling. What should the lead auditor do?
Assign the free auditor to help with the extra sampling
Send the free auditor to start drafting the final report
Add a new area to the scope so she stays productive on site
Tell the busy auditor to stop at the planned sample size

Moving people to where the audit needs them most is how a lead auditor reallocates resources on site. Stopping at the planned sample ignores evidence that a wider problem may exist, and scope changes need client agreement.
std
II.B.1
On day one, the team learns that plating, listed in the plan as an internal process, is outsourced. What should the lead auditor do?
Keep the plan as is and record plating as not done
Raise a nonconformity against the auditee for supplying wrong information
Agree with the client and auditee how to revise the plan
Visit the plating supplier's site the next day
When facts on site change the basis of the plan, the lead auditor reassesses it and agrees changes with the client and auditee. Visiting the supplier would go beyond the agreed scope.
std
II.B.1
On day one, the team finds that most records needed to meet the audit objectives are held at another site outside the scope. What should the lead auditor do?
Continue as planned and leave the problem out of the final report
Report the problem to the client and auditee to decide next steps
Travel to the other site the next day without asking anyone
Rate every requirement that relies on those records as met

If the audit objectives may not be achievable, the lead auditor tells the client and auditee so they can decide whether to change the plan, scope or objectives. Continuing silently would produce conclusions the evidence cannot support.
std
II.B.1
A sub-assembly interview set for day one has moved to day two because the area manager is away. What is the best adjustment?
Bring forward day-two work and update the team schedule
Leave day one partly idle and keep the plan unchanged
Hold the interview with whoever happens to be free in the area
Cancel the interview and rely on the records instead
Swapping planned activities keeps the team productive while the needed person is unavailable. Cancelling or substituting an uninformed interviewee lowers the quality of evidence.
std
II.B.1
How should a lead auditor keep the auditee informed during a multi-day audit?
Have each auditor tell operators about their findings as they go
Hold the results until the closing meeting
Hold short daily meetings on progress and concerns
Send the auditee the draft report each evening

Regular briefings let the auditee hear concerns early, supply more evidence and avoid surprises at the end. Holding everything until closing denies the auditee the chance to respond while the team is still on site.
std
II.B.1
On day two, an auditor finds a significant nonconformity in shipping. When should the auditee first hear of it?
In the final report, after the team reviews it
When the auditee asks about the shipping area
Promptly, at the daily briefing or sooner
At the closing meeting with all other findings

Significant concerns are communicated during the audit so the auditee can respond and so the closing meeting holds no surprises. Saving them for the closing meeting removes the chance to clarify or provide more evidence.
std
II.B.2
The quality manager is the auditee's representative for a customer audit. Which task is part of her role?
Act as the link between the auditors and site management
Decide which findings the auditors may report
Answer the auditors' questions on behalf of the operators being interviewed
Write the audit report on behalf of the auditors

The auditee representative coordinates between the audit team and management, arranging people, records and access. Controlling what is reported or answering for operators would interfere with the auditors' independence.
std
II.B.2
A site is preparing to host a three-day certification audit. Which preparation helps the audit most?
Coach employees on scripted answers to the questions auditors usually ask
Ask staff in the audited areas to take those days off
Move nonconforming material out of sight before the visit
Brief guides and ensure key people and records will be available
Good auditee preparation makes the audit run smoothly by having guides ready and people and records on hand. Scripting answers or hiding material misleads the auditors and is an ethical breach.
std
II.B.2
A guide accompanies an external auditor through production. An operator hesitates over a question. What should the guide do?
Answer for the operator to avoid mistakes
Remind the operator of what the written procedure says to do
Suggest the auditor move on to another area
Let the operator answer, adding context only if asked

Guides accompany auditors to help and observe, not to answer for the people being interviewed. Prompting or answering for the operator makes the evidence about the guide rather than the operator's practice.
std
II.B.2
An auditor asks why a lot was released without final test. The auditee representative knows a signed customer deviation covers it. What should she do?
Tell the auditor the issue is outside the scope of the audit
Wait until the closing meeting to bring it up
Give the deviation to the auditor promptly for review
Ask the auditor to drop the question for now

Providing clarifying information while the team is on site lets the auditor weigh all the evidence before reaching a conclusion. Waiting until closing makes a dispute more likely and leaves less time to check the document.
std
II.B.2
At a daily briefing, an auditor presents a nonconformity that the auditee believes is wrong because the record is in another file. What is the best response?
Produce the record during the audit so the auditor can recheck
Refuse to sign the attendance sheet at the closing meeting in protest
Accept the finding now and dispute it in the action response
Complain to the auditor's employer after the audit is over

The auditee may dispute a finding, and the right way is to give the auditor the evidence while it can still be checked on site. Disputes raised after the audit are harder to resolve and may leave an incorrect finding on record.
std
II.B.2
Why should the auditee confirm the facts behind each finding while the audit is under way?
It is needed before the auditor may record evidence
It allows the auditee to lower the finding's grade
It shows that the auditee accepts the auditor's conclusion as well
It prevents later disputes and supports sound corrective action
Agreeing on the facts during the audit means corrective action starts from an accurate problem statement. Confirming facts is not the same as accepting the auditor's classification of them.
std
II.B.3
At the opening meeting, the plant manager asks why the audit covers only two of the site's five product lines. What should the lead auditor do?
Expand the scope to all five lines on the spot to satisfy him
Tell him that scope is not discussed at this meeting
Explain the purpose and how it led to the agreed scope
Refer him to the quality manager for an answer
Confirming purpose and scope is a core task of the opening meeting, and questions about them should be answered there. Changing the scope on the spot requires the client's agreement.
std
II.B.3
Why should the lead auditor explain at the opening meeting how findings will be graded?
So the team can leave grades out of the report
So the auditee knows roughly how many findings to expect from the team
So the auditee can agree on grades in advance
So the auditee knows how major and minor findings differ

Explaining the grading scheme up front lets the auditee understand what each classification means and what response it will require. Grades depend on evidence not yet gathered, so they cannot be agreed in advance.
std
II.B.3
Why does the lead auditor keep a record of who attended the opening meeting?
It is used to grade management commitment
It replaces the plan's distribution list
It shows who was told the audit's purpose, scope and methods
It lists the people the auditors are not permitted to interview
An attendance record documents which auditee people were informed of how the audit would run, which helps if questions arise later. It has nothing to do with who may be interviewed.
std
II.B.3
At the opening meeting, the auditee says the press area supervisor is out on day one. What should the lead auditor do?
Move the press area to day two and confirm the revised schedule
Audit the press area on day one as planned, without the supervisor
Remove the press area from the audit scope
Postpone the whole audit until he returns

Reviewing the schedule at the opening meeting lets the team adjust for availability while keeping the scope intact. Removing the area or postponing the audit is an overreaction to a simple scheduling issue.
std
II.B.3
At the opening meeting, an attendee asks whether auditors will look at personnel files. What is the best response?
Answer from the agreed plan and resolve any concern now
Ask for the question in writing after the meeting
Say that auditors decide on the spot what records they will review
Defer the questions to the closing meeting
The opening meeting is the place to clear up questions so the audit can proceed smoothly. Deferring questions leaves concerns that can disrupt the audit later.
std
II.B.4
An auditor wants to learn how an operator handles a gauge that fails its daily check. What is the best interviewing approach?
Ask open questions at her workstation and have her show the steps
Hand her the written procedure and ask whether she follows it step by step
Ask yes-or-no questions to keep the interview short
Ask her supervisor to explain while she listens nearby

Open questions asked where the work happens, with the person showing what she does, produce the most reliable interview evidence. Yes-or-no or leading questions invite the answer the interviewee thinks the auditor wants.
std
II.B.4
An interviewee's description of a task conflicts with the written procedure. What should the auditor do next?
Have the employee sign a statement of what was said in the interview
Record a nonconformity based on the interview statement alone
Accept the description, since operators know the job best
Check records or watch the task to see what is done
Interview statements are verified against other sources before they are used as a basis for a finding. Writing a nonconformity from one statement risks citing a misunderstanding.
std
II.B.4
Which audit check is best done by observing work activities?
Whether supplier approval dates are kept in the database
Whether operators verify the first piece before running a lot
Whether the last management review covered audit results
Whether top management approved the current quality policy statement
First-piece verification is a task done at the workstation, so watching it gives direct evidence. The other checks concern records and are best answered by examining documents.
std
II.B.4
An auditor wants to confirm that an accepted part on the shelf meets a critical diameter. Which approach gives the strongest evidence?
Ask the inspector whether that part was checked at final
Review the inspection record for that lot of parts
Have the part measured with a calibrated gauge
Compare it by eye with a known good part from stock

A measurement with suitable, calibrated equipment directly shows whether the characteristic conforms. The inspection record shows only what was recorded, not whether the part on the shelf actually meets the drawing.
std
II.B.4
When an auditor takes physical measurements, what must be true for the results to be valid evidence?
The parts were chosen by the area supervisor
The gauge used is suitable and calibrated
The results agree with the inspection records
More readings were taken than the inspector took

Measurement evidence is only as good as the equipment used, so it must be capable of the needed resolution and calibrated. Requiring agreement with the auditee's records would defeat the point of an independent check.
std
II.B.4
Which document gives the strongest evidence that a training requirement is being met?
The approved training budget for the current year
Training records for a sample of operators in the job
The training calendar the department has planned for next quarter
The procedure that describes the training process
Records for a sample of the people doing the job show whether the requirement was actually met. A procedure, budget or calendar shows intent, not completion.
std
II.B.4
An auditor has notes from interviews, observations and records. Before writing findings, what should she evaluate?
Whether the items fit the number of findings she expected to raise
Whether each item is relevant, reliable and sufficient
Whether each item came from a senior employee
Whether the auditee's manager shares her opinion

Information becomes audit evidence only if it relates to the criteria, can be relied on and is enough to support a conclusion. Agreement from management or seniority of the source does not make information reliable.
std
II.B.4
An auditor overhears a forklift driver say that labels are often wrong. Nothing else supports this yet. How should it be treated?
As a nonconformity, since an employee reported it directly
As irrelevant, since forklift drivers are out of scope
As an observation to be listed in the final report
As a lead to check, not yet as audit evidence
An unverified remark is hearsay; it can point the auditor where to look, but it becomes evidence only if checked. Writing a finding from it, or ignoring it, are both poor uses of the information.
std
II.B.5
An auditor watches an operator skip a required leak test on two parts. How is this evidence best described?
Observed
Confirmed
Documented
Corroborated
The auditor saw the event directly, which makes it observed evidence. Corroborated evidence is a statement or fact supported by a second, independent source.
std
II.B.5
An auditor checks five parts with a calibrated micrometer and finds two over the upper limit. How is this evidence best described?
Corroborated
Measured
Documented
Confirmed
Evidence obtained by the auditor using measuring equipment is measured evidence. It is not documented evidence, which comes from records the auditee already holds.
std
II.B.5
An auditor shows the area manager the facts she gathered on the line, and the manager agrees they are accurate. How is the evidence now best described?
Confirmed
Observed
Documented
Measured
When the responsible person agrees that the facts are accurate, the evidence is confirmed. Agreement does not create a record, so it is not documented evidence.
std
II.B.5
An operator says rework is often done without a ticket. The auditor then finds three reworked parts with no ticket in the rework log. How is the operator's statement now best described?
Documented
Corroborated
Observed
Measured
A statement supported by a second, independent source, here the rework log, is corroborated. The log itself is documented evidence, but the term for the operator's statement is corroborated.
std
II.B.5
Which of these is documented objective evidence?
An auditor's belief that training is weak
A rumor in the break room that a gauge fell
A supervisor's estimate that most lots pass final test the first time
A signed inspection record showing a failed test
A signed record of a test result is factual and verifiable, which makes it documented objective evidence. Beliefs, estimates and rumors are opinion or hearsay until verified.
std
II.B.5
Which statement is objective evidence?
Three of ten sampled orders lacked an approval signature
The approval process seems poorly understood by staff
Staff do not appear to care much about signatures
Approvals are probably skipped whenever the team is busy at month end
Objective evidence is verifiable fact, such as a count from a defined sample. The other statements are the auditor's interpretations, which need facts behind them.
std
II.B.5
A supervisor tells an auditor that all lots last month passed final test. What must happen before this becomes objective evidence?
It must be written down in the auditor's notes
It must be stated again at the closing meeting
It must be verified against the test records
It must be repeated by a second supervisor
A statement becomes objective evidence when it is verified by observation, measurement or records. Writing it down or hearing it twice from the same chain of command does not verify it.
std
II.B.6
One auditor finds a late calibration on a gauge used only to sort scrap. Another finds no current drawing at the inspection station for a safety-critical part. Which finding is more significant?
The missing drawing at the safety-critical inspection station
Both equally, since each breaks a stated requirement
The late calibration, since calibration is a formal requirement
Neither, since each is a single instance of a lapse

Significance depends on what the lapse could affect, and inspecting a safety-critical part without the current drawing threatens product conformity directly. A late calibration on a scrap-sorting gauge has little effect on product.
std
II.B.6
Which finding is most severe?
An unused obsolete form found in a desk drawer in planning
An internal phone list updated a month later than planned
Nonconforming brake parts shipped to a customer
A training record filed in the wrong folder in the office

Severity reflects the seriousness of the consequence, and nonconforming safety parts at a customer have the gravest one. The others are administrative lapses with little effect on product or customer.
std
II.B.6
In 30 sampled travelers, an auditor finds nine missing inspection stamps spread across all three shifts. What does this frequency suggest?
An isolated error by one inspector
A sampling quirk that should be set aside
A problem confined to the inspectors on one of the shifts
A systemic breakdown rather than an isolated slip
Nearly a third of the sample, spread across every shift, points to a weakness in the system rather than one person's mistake. The spread rules out a single shift or inspector.
std
II.B.6
Two findings occur at similar frequency. One involves a process whose failure could injure users; the other affects only cosmetic appearance. How should they be ranked?
In the order in which the auditors found them
By the size of the workforce in each area
Equally, since their frequency is the same
The injury-related finding ranks first
Risk combines likelihood with the consequence, so equal frequency with a far worse outcome means higher risk. Ranking by order found or headcount ignores consequence.
std
II.B.6
An auditor finds that an uncontrolled spreadsheet is used to set heat-treat cycle times for every part family. Why is this best treated as a system issue?
System issues need less corrective action
It can affect many parts and processes, not one lot
Spreadsheets are outside product requirements
Product issues cannot be raised as findings in a system audit

A tool that drives a process for every part family can affect many products, so the weakness lies in how the system controls such tools. Treating it as a single product defect would miss the wider exposure.
std
II.B.6
An auditor finds that scrap from a poorly controlled process has tripled this year. How can she best express its impact to management?
Describe it as a prevention cost the site chose
Tie it to the appraisal cost of the audit itself
Tie it to the rise in internal failure costs
Leave cost out, since it is outside quality audits
Scrap is an internal failure cost, and expressing a finding in cost of quality terms helps management weigh it against other priorities. Appraisal and prevention are different cost categories.
std
II.B.6
An auditor finds one expired adhesive at a workstation within scope, and time remains in the schedule. What should she do?
Ignore it, since one case is not significant
Check other workstations in scope to see if it is isolated
Extend the audit to similar workstations at sites outside the scope
Raise a major nonconformity right away
A single instance may be isolated or a sign of a wider problem, so the auditor samples further within scope before classifying it. Extending into sites outside the scope needs the client's agreement.
std
II.B.6
While auditing, an auditor sees evidence of a problem in an area outside the audit scope. What should she do?
Ignore it, since it falls outside the scope
Tell the lead auditor so it can be reported to the client
Write it up as a nonconformity in the report for this audit
Extend her audit into that area on her own

Matters outside scope are passed on through the lead auditor so the client can decide on action. Auditing it unilaterally changes the scope without agreement, and writing it up as a finding lacks the planned basis.
std
II.B.7
Why does the lead auditor restate the purpose, scope and grading criteria at the closing meeting?
To let the auditee change the grade of findings
To frame results for attendees who missed the opening
To reopen the scope so areas not yet audited can be added
To fill time while the report is being typed
Restating the basis of the audit helps everyone present understand the results in context, especially people who were not at the opening. It is not a chance to renegotiate scope or grades.
std
II.B.7
A month after an audit, a department manager says he was never told of a finding in his area. Which record would best settle this?
The attendance record for the closing meeting
The opening meeting agenda
The audit plan sent before the audit
The audit checklist the auditor used in his area
A record of who attended the closing meeting shows who was present when results were presented. The plan and agenda were issued before any findings existed.
std
II.B.7
How should results be presented at the closing meeting?
As a draft subject to the auditee's approval
Positive results only, with nonconformities left to the report
Without evidence, to avoid blaming individuals
Clearly, with each finding and its evidence
The auditee must understand each finding and the evidence behind it to accept the facts and act. Leaving nonconformities for the report creates surprises and denies the auditee a chance to respond.
std
II.B.7
At the closing meeting, the auditee agrees that the records were missing but disagrees that this is a nonconformity. What should the lead auditor do?
Downgrade the finding to an observation
Withdraw the finding, since there is no agreement
Delay the closing meeting until the auditee agrees to it
Record the agreed facts and note the differing views

The aim is agreement on the evidence; the auditee need not accept the conclusion, and unresolved differences are recorded. Withdrawing or downgrading because of disagreement would let the auditee decide the result.
std
II.B.7
What concurrence does the lead auditor seek at the closing meeting?
Agreement on the root cause of each finding
Agreement on the grade given to each finding
Agreement on the facts behind each finding
Agreement on dates for every corrective action
Concurrence on the evidence means the auditee cannot later claim the facts were wrong. Grading is the auditor's call, and root causes and action dates come later from the auditee.
std
II.B.7
The team could not review calibration records because the system was down during the audit. What should be agreed at the closing meeting?
That calibration is dropped without comment
That calibration is recorded as conforming for this audit cycle
That the auditee writes the calibration finding
How and when the missing evidence will be gathered

When part of the scope could not be covered, the closing meeting agrees how the remaining evidence will be obtained, such as a follow-up visit or submitted records. Calling it conforming without evidence would be false.
std
II.B.7
The lead auditor says a follow-up audit will verify the actions on two major findings. What else should the closing meeting make clear?
Which auditor will write each of the corrective actions
Which employees caused each of the findings in the area
Who is responsible for each action and by when
How the auditee can avoid having a follow-up audit
Next steps only work if each has an owner and a date. Corrective actions belong to the auditee, not the auditor, and assigning personal blame is not the purpose of the meeting.
std
II.B.7
At the closing meeting, an auditee manager asks who will develop corrective actions for the findings. What is the correct answer?
The technical expert who supported the team
The auditee plans and carries out the corrective actions
The lead auditor, who knows the evidence behind the findings best
The audit client's purchasing manager
Responsibility for corrective action rests with the auditee, who owns the process. Auditors who design the fix would later be auditing their own solution.
std
II.C.1
During an internal audit, three operators on different shifts were each found running a press to a superseded revision of the same work instruction. How should the lead auditor report this?
As one document control finding with all three instances as evidence
As three separate nonconformities, one for each operator and each shift
As an observation only, since each operator followed the document at hand
As an opportunity for improvement to retrain operators on revision checks

The three instances share one requirement and one likely system cause, so grouping them into a single finding with the instances as evidence makes it actionable and shows the extent of the problem. Splitting them by operator points the auditee at individuals and invites three narrow fixes instead of one system fix.
std
II.C.1

An audit produced two nonconformities: one training record is missing a supervisor signature, and torque wrenches used on safety-critical fasteners are four months past calibration. How should the report treat them?
Rate the torque wrench finding higher and present it first in the results
Rate the training record higher, since records show system discipline
Rate both the same, since each one fails to meet a stated requirement
Drop the training record, since one missing signature is not significant

Severity follows the risk to product and people: uncalibrated tools on safety-critical joints could let unsafe product ship, while a missing signature has little direct impact. Rating them equally ignores significance, which a report is expected to highlight.
std
II.C.1

On behalf of its purchasing department, a manufacturer audits a supplier and finds that raw material lot numbers are not recorded at the extrusion line. When the auditor states the risk of this finding, what is most relevant?
The supplier's record keeping falls short of good industry practice
Neither client nor supplier could isolate suspect lots
The supplier's operators were not trained on the lot recording form
The finding would also be cited by a certification body auditor

Risk is stated in terms of consequence to the client and the auditee: without traceability, neither can contain or recall suspect material if a defect appears. Training gaps and practice comparisons describe causes or context, not the risk itself.
std
II.C.1
After a four-day audit, the lead auditor has notes and evidence from four team members covering 11 processes. What should she do first to develop the report?
Write the executive summary so the main message is fixed early on
Send all the team notes to the auditee to confirm their accuracy
Attach the notes word for word as an appendix to the audit report
Sort the notes by process and criterion and merge duplicate evidence
Organizing and consolidating the raw material comes first; the summary and conclusions are written from that organized base. Writing the summary first risks a message the evidence does not support.
std
II.C.1
While drafting the report, the lead auditor finds evidence in her notes of a nonconformity that was not raised at the closing meeting. What should she do?
Add it to the report, since the objective evidence fully supports it
Discuss it with the auditee before it goes into the report
Leave it out and record it in her notes for the next scheduled audit
Hold the entire report until a special audit can confirm the problem

Finalizing results means the report should hold no surprises: anything not presented at the closing meeting is shared with the auditee before it appears in the report. Adding it unannounced damages trust, and silently dropping supported evidence leaves a known problem unreported.
std
II.C.1
An audit found 14 minor documentation lapses and one major nonconformity: final functional testing was being skipped on rush orders. How should the report be built?
Feature the major finding in the summary and lead with it
List the findings in the order the team discovered them on site
List all 15 findings in clause order and give each equal weight
Put the major finding in an appendix to keep the report balanced

Critical issues must stand out so management acts on them first; untested product reaching customers is far more serious than the paperwork lapses. Clause order or discovery order buries the issue that matters most.
std
II.C.1
An audit program assigns each finding a code such as IA-26-04-07. What is the main purpose of this practice?
To let each finding be tracked to closure
To show which auditor wrote the finding
To rank the findings in order of severity
To meet a coding rule set out in ISO 9001

A unique identifier links the finding to its corrective action request, response, verification and closure records so nothing is lost. ISO 9001 requires audit results to be retained but does not prescribe a coding scheme.
std
II.C.1
A draft finding reads: "Calibration is poorly controlled in the plant." Which rewrite makes it actionable?
Three of 12 receiving gauges sampled were past due, contrary to procedure QP-12
Several gauges looked old or damaged and should be replaced as soon as possible
Calibration control is weak and needs urgent management attention plantwide
Calibration was discussed with the technician, who agreed it needs improvement

An actionable finding states the requirement, the objective evidence and the gap so the auditee knows exactly what to correct and can investigate the extent. The other versions are opinions or impressions with no traceable evidence.
std
II.C.2
Which content belongs in the background section of an audit report?
Objectives, scope, criteria, dates, team members and auditee contacts
The findings ranked by severity, with the evidence for each of them
The corrective actions the auditee has agreed to take for each finding
The auditor's recommended fixes for each finding and their likely cost
Background sets the frame for the audit: why, what, against which criteria, when and by whom. Findings belong in the results section, and auditors report gaps rather than prescribing fixes.
std
II.C.2
The plant manager will read only the first page of an audit report. What should the executive summary on that page contain?
The detailed evidence behind every finding with its record numbers
A list of everyone interviewed and the processes each person runs
The audit method, the sampling plan and the checklists that were used
The overall conclusion, the most significant findings and responses due
An executive summary gives a busy reader the conclusion, what matters most and what action is expected. Detailed evidence, interview lists and methods belong in the body or appendices.
std
II.C.2
No requirement is being violated yet, but the auditor sees that the gauge recall list is updated by hand and was nearly missed twice last quarter. How is this best reported?
As a minor nonconformity against the calibration procedure
As an observation that could lead to a nonconformity later
As a major nonconformity, because it may well get much worse
Not at all, since only nonconformities are included in reports

An observation records a condition that meets requirements today but could lead to a nonconformity, so the auditee can act before it happens. Calling it a nonconformity of any grade is not supported, because no requirement has been missed.
std
II.C.2
How should the results section of an audit report be ordered?
Alphabetically by department, so each manager can find his own area
By the order in which the audit team discovered each issue on site
By clause number of the standard, regardless of severity or risk
Major nonconformities first, then minors, observations, OFIs

Prioritized results put the issues with the greatest risk where readers see them first and act on them first. Ordering by department, discovery or clause can hide a serious finding among routine ones.
std
II.C.2
A process fully meets its requirements, but the auditor notices that two inspection steps check the same features. How should this appear in the report?
As an opportunity for improvement, with no corrective action needed
As a minor nonconformity that requires a full root cause analysis
As a finding with the auditor's chosen fix and a deadline for it
It should be left out, since only gaps belong in an audit report

An opportunity for improvement notes a possible gain where requirements are met; the auditee decides whether and how to act. Treating it as a nonconformity or dictating a fix goes beyond what the evidence and the auditor's role support.
std
II.C.2
A reviewer finds that a draft report uses long narrative paragraphs, mixes facts with opinion, and names two operators who made errors. Which revision most improves it?
Quote each interview in full so readers can judge every statement
Keep the operator names so managers know who needs retraining now
Add more descriptive wording so the seriousness is clear to readers
Use one format per finding with requirement, evidence and the gap

A consistent, factual format citing the requirement and the evidence is clear and defensible, and reports address the system rather than blaming individuals. Long quotes and stronger wording add volume without adding clarity.
std
II.C.2
An audit across six departments produced 40 findings, and the lead auditor wants to show that most of them relate to document control. Which tool best highlights this conclusion?
A control chart of findings by auditor
A Pareto chart of findings by category
A scatter diagram of findings by date
A cause and effect diagram of findings

A Pareto chart ranks categories by frequency, so the dominance of document control is visible at a glance. A cause and effect diagram explores possible causes of one problem; it does not show which category of finding is most frequent.
std
II.C.2
An auditee manager reads the final report and asks when corrective action responses are due. The report does not say. What should the report have included?
A response due date per the program procedure, such as 30 days
No dates, because the timing of corrective action is the auditee's
Implementation dates for each fix, set by the lead auditor alone
A note that response dates will be set at the next planned audit

An effective report sets a timeline for the auditee's response and corrective action plan, normally per the audit program's procedure. Leaving it open or deferring it to the next audit lets findings drift.
std
II.C.2

A draft report's executive summary says the quality system is "effective and well maintained," yet the results include a major finding that untested product was shipped. What is the most serious weakness of this draft?
The background section lists every member of the audit team by name
The results present the findings in tables instead of in narrative form
The summary's conclusion is contradicted by the major finding it omits
The report lists the opportunities for improvement after the findings
The executive summary must reflect the evidence; a summary that omits a major finding misleads the readers most likely to act on it. Tables, team lists and putting OFIs last are normal practice.
std
II.C.3

The audit procedure requires the audit program manager to approve each report before release. He is away for a week, and the auditee presses the lead auditor to send the report today. What should she do?
Send it now marked final and get the approval after he returns
Have the auditee's manager approve it so it can be sent today
Send the unapproved draft but label it as subject to change
Use the alternate approver the procedure names, or else wait

Required approvals are part of issuing the report, so the lead auditor follows the procedure, including any named alternate. Letting the auditee approve the report it is the subject of defeats the independence of the review.
std
II.C.3
A manufacturer audits a supplier, and the supplier's other customer later asks the lead auditor for a copy of the report. What is the right response?
Send it, since the findings concern the supplier rather than the client
Send a summary only, with the names and details of the parts removed
Refer the request to the audit client, as the report is confidential
Ask the supplier to approve the release and then send it if they agree

The report belongs to the audit client and goes only to recipients on the agreed distribution list, so any other request goes back to the client. The supplier's consent alone does not override the client's control of its own report.
std
II.C.3
Who should normally receive the final report of an internal process audit?
Every employee, through a posting on the plant notice board
The lead auditor only, who then decides who may read it
The certification body, sent automatically on the issue date
The people on the distribution list set by the procedure

Distribution follows established procedures, usually the auditee managers responsible for the area and the audit program manager. Wide posting ignores confidentiality, and automatic copies to outside bodies are not standard practice.
std
II.C.3
Which set of records best describes the contents of a complete audit file?
The final report only, since working notes are discarded at issue
Plan, checklists, notes, evidence, report and nonconformity records
Copies of every procedure and record the audit team happened to see
The auditor training records and the auditors' annual appraisals

The audit file holds what is needed to show how the audit was planned, done and reported, and to track its findings. Copying every document seen is unnecessary, and auditor appraisals belong in personnel or competence records.
std
II.C.3
How long should an internal audit file be kept?
Until the same area is audited again
Until all of its findings are closed
For as long as the lead auditor decides
As set by the records retention policy

Retention follows the organization's records policy, including any customer or regulatory requirements. Discarding the file at the next audit or at closure can destroy evidence the policy, a customer or a regulator still expects to see.
std
II.D.1
The response to a finding about an expired gauge reads: "The gauge was recalibrated and returned to service." How should the auditor evaluate it?
Acceptable, since the gauge in question now meets requirements
Acceptable once the auditee attaches the new calibration record
Incomplete, since cause and recurrence are not addressed
Incomplete, since the auditee should have replaced the gauge

Recalibrating the gauge is a correction; a corrective action response also needs the cause of the lapse and action to stop it happening again, plus a look at product measured with the gauge. Attaching the record proves the correction but adds nothing about cause.
std
II.D.1
A corrective action request has sat for 60 days with "Owner: Quality Department" and no progress. What change is most likely to move it forward?
Assign it to the auditor who wrote the original finding
Assign a named manager who has authority over the process
Assign it to the operator who was working when it was found
Leave it with the Quality Department but add a new due date

A CAPA needs a named owner with authority over the process to drive problem definition and action. The auditor must stay independent of the fix, and an operator rarely has the authority to change the system.
std
II.D.1
A CAPA response states: "Root cause: operator error. Action: operator retrained." How should the auditor evaluate it?
Acceptable, because the training directly addresses the stated cause
Acceptable, as long as the operator has signed the training record
Not acceptable, because human error can never count as a root cause
Not acceptable, because it does not explain why the error was possible

Root cause analysis should ask why the system allowed the error or failed to catch it, such as unclear instructions or no error-proofing. Human error can be a contributing cause, so rejecting it outright is too absolute; the problem is that the analysis stopped too soon.
std
II.D.1
A team believes a worn locating pin is the root cause of recurring hole position defects. Which evidence best confirms it?
Most of the team members agreed on it during a brainstorming session
The pin was the most frequent cause listed on the fishbone diagram
Replacing the pin stopped the defects; refitting it restored them
The machine supplier said worn pins often cause this kind of defect
Turning a suspected cause off and on and seeing the effect follow is strong evidence of a true root cause. Votes, fishbone counts and expert opinion generate candidate causes but do not verify one.
std
II.D.1
Cartons are sometimes shipped with the wrong product label. Which action best prevents recurrence?
Issue a memo reminding packers to double-check each label
Add a final inspection to check every carton label by eye
Scan each label against the work order before it is sealed
Apply discipline to any packer who ships a wrong label again
An automatic check that will not let a mismatched label pass removes the opportunity for the error. Added visual inspection only tries to catch it after it happens and is itself prone to human error.
std
II.D.1

After fixing the cause of a sealing defect on Line 1, a plant applies the same fix to Lines 2 and 3, which use the same equipment but have had no defects. In traditional CAPA terms, the action on Lines 2 and 3 is:
A correction
A preventive action
A corrective action
A containment action

Action on the cause of a potential nonconformity that has not occurred is preventive action; ISO 9001:2015 folds this into corrective action by asking whether similar problems could occur elsewhere. It is not corrective action on those lines, because no nonconformity occurred there.
std
II.D.2
Which proposed corrective action plan for a major finding is most acceptable?
Root cause confirmed by data, actions on it, owners, dates and an effectiveness check
A list of actions with dates, and a commitment to find the root cause later this year
A detailed root cause analysis, with actions to be decided at the next management review
Immediate containment of affected stock, with no further action planned at this time

An acceptable plan ties action to a verified cause, assigns responsibility and dates, and says how effectiveness will be checked. Containment is needed but deals only with the effects, and actions planned before the cause is known may miss it.
std
II.D.2
For a finding that untested product could ship, an auditee proposes a nine-month schedule because new test equipment must be bought. How should the auditor respond?
Accept the plan as written, since the capital purchase takes time
Reject the plan and require full completion within thirty days
Accept the schedule only with immediate interim containment
Accept the plan but downgrade the finding to an observation

A long schedule can be reasonable for a capital fix, but not while risky product keeps shipping; interim controls must protect the customer until then. Demanding thirty days ignores what is achievable, and the finding's severity does not change because the fix is slow.
std
II.D.2
An auditee commits to installing a new plantwide traceability system within two weeks of a finding. What is the auditor's best response?
Accept the date, since a quick commitment shows strong intent
Ask for a milestone plan with realistic dates and interim steps
Reject it and set a six-month due date for the auditee instead
Accept it and plan to check progress at the next annual audit

A schedule must be realistic as well as prompt; an unachievable date leads to missed commitments, so milestones and interim measures make the plan credible. The auditor evaluates the schedule but does not impose dates of his own.
std
II.D.2
An auditee insists that retraining is enough to address a recurring nonconformity, though the auditor sees no cause analysis behind it. Which negotiating approach is best?
Write a full corrective action plan for the auditee to sign off
Accept the retraining plan to keep the working relationship good
Escalate at once to the chief executive to force a change in plan
Show the evidence of recurrence and ask how retraining stops it

Grounding the discussion in the evidence and the requirement, and asking the auditee to show how the plan addresses cause, keeps ownership with the auditee while holding the standard. Writing the plan for them compromises the auditor's independence.
std
II.D.2
An auditee says a corrective action date is impossible because capital requests are approved only each quarter. Which outcome is the best negotiated result?
Keep the original date and record any slip as a new finding
A phased plan with containment now and dates for each phase
An open-ended extension until the capital funds are approved
Withdraw the finding, since the cause is outside their control

A phased plan with interim controls and milestones meets the real constraint while keeping risk managed and progress visible. Open-ended extensions remove accountability, and withdrawing a valid finding misstates the audit results.
std
II.D.3
An auditee reports that a procedure was revised to fix a finding. What is the best way to verify this?
Accept the email from the auditee confirming the revision was made
Confirm the procedure's revision number has changed in the index
Check the content addresses the cause, is approved and is in use
Ask the procedure's author to sign a statement that it is complete

Verification checks that the revised content actually addresses the cause, is properly approved and issued, and that people are using it. A changed revision number shows something changed, not that the change is adequate or in use.
std
II.D.3
A corrective action added a setup verification step on a stamping press. Which verification gives the strongest evidence that it is in place?
Watching operators do the step and checking setup records
Confirming that the work instruction was revised to add the step
Asking the supervisor whether operators are doing the new step
Reviewing the training sign-off sheet for the press operators
Observing the revised process and sampling its records shows the change is actually practiced. A revised instruction or training record shows intent, not that the step happens on the floor.
std
II.D.3
Which corrective action most warrants an on-site follow-up audit rather than a desk review of submitted evidence?
A misspelled part number corrected in one controlled work instruction
A new form added to record supplier approvals, sent with its first entry
A clarified retention period in the records procedure, sent as a copy
A revised heat treat process for a major finding on product hardness
A major finding that depends on how a process actually runs needs to be seen in operation. Simple document fixes can be verified by reviewing the submitted documents.
std
II.D.3
Two weeks after a corrective action was put in place for a recurring weld defect, the auditee asks to close it. Records show the new controls are in use. What should the auditor do?
Close it, because the new controls are confirmed in use
Close it, and reopen it only if a customer complains again
Keep it open and plan a check of effectiveness over time
Keep it open until the next annual audit of the weld area
Implementation is confirmed, but effectiveness needs evidence over enough production that the defect does not recur. Waiting for the next annual audit delays the check far beyond what is needed.
std
II.D.3

A supplier claims its corrective action for a cracking defect worked. The defect rate was 4.0% over the six months before the change and 3.8% over the three months since. How should the auditor evaluate this?
Effective, because the defect rate has fallen since the change
Effective, because three months of data is enough for any change
Not yet shown effective, since the rate is about the same as before
Not effective, because the defect rate has failed to reach zero

A drop from 4.0% to 3.8% is small and the post-change period is short, so without evidence that the change is more than ordinary variation the data do not show the cause was removed. Effectiveness does not always demand zero defects; it demands evidence of real, sustained improvement against the problem.
std
II.D.4
A corrective action response is 60 days overdue, and two reminders to the area manager have gone unanswered. What is the best next step?
Close the request and note the lack of response in the file
Escalate to the manager's superior per the audit procedure
Have the auditor carry out the corrective action instead
Issue a fresh finding each week until a response arrives

When a CAPA is not being implemented and normal follow-up fails, the audit program escalates to a level of management with authority over the area. Closing it hides an open risk, and an auditor doing the fix loses independence.
std
II.D.4
At verification, the auditor finds the same nonconformity recurring on the line even though the corrective action was carried out as planned. What should he do?
Accept closure, since the action was carried out exactly as planned
Escalate the matter at once to the chief executive of the auditee
Reject closure and require the root cause analysis to be repeated
Schedule a full system re-audit covering every process on the site

Recurrence after faithful implementation means the cause was wrong or incomplete, so the CAPA is ineffective and the analysis must be redone. Completing the plan is not the goal; removing the problem is.
std
II.D.4
Which situation most clearly justifies escalating a corrective action to higher management?
The auditee asks for a one-week extension and explains the delay
A response to a minor finding contains a typing error in one date
The auditee disagrees with the wording used in one of the findings
Commitments keep slipping and the manager says no resources exist

Escalation fits when the issue is beyond the auditee manager's authority, such as missing resources, and repeated commitments are missed. A reasonable extension request or a wording dispute can be handled at the working level.
std
II.D.4
A supplier's response describes a thorough fix for a packaging problem, but the finding concerned missing heat treat certifications. What is the most appropriate action?
Reissue the request with a clearer problem statement and evidence
Accept the response, since the packaging fix is still worthwhile
Close the finding and raise a new finding about the supplier's reply
Remove the supplier from the approved list for failing to respond

The supplier answered the wrong problem, which points to an unclear request; reissuing it with a precise statement and evidence restarts the CAPA on the right issue. Accepting an unrelated fix leaves the real nonconformity open.
std
II.D.4
A supplier says corrective actions for four major findings are complete, but the records it sent conflict with one another and show dates before the audit. What should the audit program do?
Accept the records, since the supplier has formally claimed closure
Re-audit the affected processes on site to verify the actions
Remove the supplier from the approved list without further review
Extend all of the due dates so the supplier can resend its records
When submitted evidence cannot be trusted and the findings are major, a re-audit lets the auditor see the actions first-hand. Disqualifying the supplier before the facts are known is premature.
std
II.D.4
The audit program finds that 40% of corrective action requests across the plant are overdue and several closed ones have recurred. Which strategy best addresses this?
Report the trend with data at management review and agree accountability
Have the auditors take over the overdue corrective actions to clear them
Lengthen every corrective action due date so fewer of them show overdue
Stop issuing requests for minor findings until the overdue backlog clears

A program-wide pattern of late and ineffective CAPA is a management system issue, so it goes to top management with data and an agreed way to hold owners accountable. Stretching due dates hides the problem rather than fixing it.
std
II.D.5

An audit procedure states that an audit is closed when all corrective actions are verified effective. Four of five findings are verified; the fifth is implemented but its effectiveness check is pending. What is the audit's status?
Closed, because most of its findings are verified
Closed, with the fifth action moved to the next audit
Open until the fifth effectiveness check is complete
Open until all of the findings are audited a second time
Under the stated criterion, closure requires every corrective action to be verified effective, so the audit stays open. Moving the item to the next audit contradicts the procedure's own closure rule.
std
II.D.5
All corrective actions from an audit have been verified effective. What remains to close the audit?
Schedule the next audit of the area within the next 30 days
Ask the auditee to sign and approve the original audit report
Destroy the working notes, since the evidence is now verified
Record the closure, notify the auditee and client, and file it

Closure is a documented step: the closure is recorded, the interested parties are told, and the records go to the audit file. Destroying working notes may breach retention rules, and the auditee does not approve the report.
std
II.D.5
Under ISO 19011:2018, when is an audit considered completed?
When all the corrective actions it led to are verified as effective
When the auditee has accepted every finding in the final report
When planned activities are done, or as agreed with the client
When the certification body has reviewed and filed the audit report

ISO 19011 treats the audit as complete once the planned activities are carried out or as otherwise agreed with the client; follow-up of actions is usually not part of the audit unless the plan says so. Many audit programs add CAPA verification to their own closure criteria, which is why the procedure must define it.
std
II.D.5
An auditor has verified the last corrective action from an audit. Which record best supports closing that finding?
An email from the auditee saying that all actions are now done
A closure entry with verifier, date, evidence seen and the result
A copy of the original finding, stamped closed by the auditee
A note in the auditor's diary that the actions looked complete

A closure record should show who verified the action, when, what evidence was examined and whether the action was effective, linked to the finding's identifier. An auditee's own statement or stamp is not independent verification.
std
III.A
An auditor notices that the machine operator she is interviewing is tense and giving one-word answers. What should she do first?
Note the tension in her records as a sign that he was not trained on the job
Ask his supervisor to come over and answer the remaining questions for him
Explain that the audit is about the process, not him, and ease in
Speed through the checklist so he spends as little time with her as possible
Putting the auditee at ease is a basic interpersonal skill and makes the answers more reliable. Recording nervousness as evidence of poor training draws a conclusion that nothing supports.
std
III.A
During a process audit, the scrap total in the monthly quality report does not match the sum of the scrap tags for the same month. Which response best shows problem-solving ability?
Write a nonconformity for falsified data before leaving the area
Accept the report figure, since the plant manager approved it
Trace sample tags into the report to see where they diverge
Ask for a corrected report by email and close the item for now
An effective auditor follows the trail to find the cause of a discrepancy before drawing a conclusion. Calling it falsified data jumps to a conclusion the evidence does not yet support.
std
III.A
An auditor must confirm that an operator was qualified before running a new laser welding cell alone. Which check best shows attention to detail?
Confirming that the training record is kept in the department's controlled filing system
Checking that his sign-off date comes before the date he first ran the cell alone
Confirming that the training form has the correct title and revision of the work instruction
Asking the operator whether he feels confident running the laser welding cell by himself

The requirement is that he was qualified before working alone, so the dates must line up; catching that kind of detail is what separates a careful check from a surface one. A correct form title shows document control, not that training came first.
std
III.A
An auditor is visiting a supplier abroad where staff rarely say no or disagree openly with a visitor. How should he adapt?
Confirm what people tell him by observing the work and checking records
Treat each yes as confirmed, since he asked the question directly
Press harder on each question until someone admits to a problem
Record the reluctance to disagree as a weakness in the supplier's culture

Cultural awareness means recognizing that a yes may be politeness and gathering evidence in ways that do not depend on direct disagreement. Pressing harder is likely to offend and still will not produce reliable answers.
std
III.A
A department manager tells the auditor, "We have done it this way for twenty years and never had a complaint." Which reply is the most diplomatic?
"Your track record is clear. Today I am comparing current practice with your documented method. Can we walk through it?"
"Twenty years without complaints does not matter here. What matters today is whether you follow your documented procedure."
"That is fair enough. If the process has worked for twenty years, I will skip this part of the checklist and move on."
"I will need to raise that attitude with the plant manager, since every area has to follow the documented procedures."
Diplomacy means acknowledging the person while keeping the audit on its purpose. Dismissing his experience provokes resistance, and skipping the area gives up the audit's objective.
std
III.A
An auditor on a three-person team is sent alone to audit an off-site warehouse while the others audit the main plant. Which behavior best shows she can work both independently and as part of a team?
She checks each finding with the lead auditor by phone before recording it, so the team speaks with a single voice
She covers her assigned area to plan without direction and raises links to plant processes at team meetings
She finishes early and then audits the plant's shipping dock on her own, since it is closely linked to the warehouse
She keeps her findings to herself until the closing meeting, so the rest of the team cannot influence her judgment
Working alone on an assignment while sharing what matters with the team is the balance the role calls for. Expanding into another auditor's area without coordination undermines the team's plan.
std
III.A
On day two of a three-day audit, the auditee's plant manager asks the lead auditor to skip the paint line because of a rush order. What is the best response?
Negotiate another slot for the paint line in the audit, and tell the client if it cannot be covered
Agree to skip the paint line, since the plant manager is entitled to decide what is audited at the site
Refuse any change and audit the paint line at the time shown in the plan, whatever the production impact
Audit the paint line during the rush anyway, but without letting the plant manager know beforehand

A lead auditor negotiates a workable adjustment that still meets the audit objectives and keeps the client informed of any gap in scope. The auditee cannot cut scope on its own, and rigid refusal ignores a reasonable request that can be accommodated.
std
III.A
A lead auditor has a welding engineer who is new to auditing and an experienced auditor with no welding background. Who should audit the weld shop?
The welding engineer alone, since he knows the process far better than anyone else on the team
The experienced auditor alone, since audit skills matter more than knowledge of welding
Both together, with the experienced auditor leading and the engineer judging technical evidence
The lead auditor herself, with the other two moved to reviewing documents in the office

Pairing them uses each person's strength and covers each person's weakness. Sending the engineer alone exposes his inexperience as an auditor, and sending the auditor alone leaves the technical evidence poorly judged.
std
III.A
A lead auditor sees that one team member's draft findings are vague and hard to verify. What should she do?
Rewrite his findings herself after the audit is over, without mentioning it to him, to keep the report on time
Review the drafts with him during the audit and coach him to state the requirement, the evidence and the gap
Remove him from the team for the remaining days and take over his assigned processes herself
Leave his findings as they are, since each auditor is responsible for the wording of his own findings

Directing a team means addressing weaknesses while the audit is still running so the evidence can be firmed up. Silently rewriting afterward may leave findings unsupported and does nothing to build the auditor's skill.
std
III.A
When planning, an auditee asks for a one-day audit. The lead auditor believes the scope needs two days. What is the best way to negotiate?
Accept the single day to keep a good relationship with the auditee and cover as much of the scope as time allows
Insist on two days, explaining that the length of an audit is entirely the lead auditor's decision to make
Plan two days anyway and tell the auditee about the second day once the opening meeting has started
Show how scope drives time and seek options both accept, such as a narrower scope or an added auditor
Good negotiation explains the reasoning and works toward an option that still meets the audit objectives. Quietly accepting one day risks an audit that cannot support its conclusions.
std
III.B
At the end of day one, the lead auditor sees that one auditor is well behind on her processes while another has finished his. What is the best action?
Add a day to the audit and tell the client about the extra day once the audit is over
Tell the auditor who is behind to drop her lower-risk items without noting it anywhere
Move some processes to the auditor who finished, if he has no conflict of interest
Let each auditor work at his or her own pace and report any gaps at the closing meeting
Rebalancing work among team members keeps the plan on track while protecting objectivity. Dropping items without recording it hides a gap in coverage from the client and auditee.
std
III.B
What is the main purpose of the daily audit team meeting during a multi-day audit?
To share progress and emerging findings and adjust assignments as needed
To brief the auditee's managers on the final classification of findings
To write and approve the sections of the final audit report each day
To repeat the opening meeting for auditee staff who missed the first one
Team meetings let the lead auditor see coverage, test emerging findings across areas and reassign work. Final classification and the report come later; briefing the auditee is a separate meeting.
std
III.B
The audit plan schedules an interview with the second-shift supervisor at 9:00 a.m. What should the lead auditor do?
Agree with the auditee to move the interview to second-shift hours
Interview the first-shift supervisor at 9:00 a.m. in his place
Ask the second-shift supervisor to come in early on audit day
Drop the second shift from the scope to keep the plan as written

Activities should be scheduled when the work and the people actually happen, so the plan is adjusted with the auditee's agreement. The first-shift supervisor cannot provide evidence about second-shift practice.
std
III.B
On day two, the process owner for purchasing is called away for a customer emergency and will be back the next morning. What is the best adjustment?
Move another activity forward and do purchasing when she returns
Interview her deputy and record the process owner as having been interviewed
Postpone the whole audit until the process owner has returned to the site
Leave purchasing out of the audit and mention the gap in the final report
Swapping activities keeps the audit moving and still covers purchasing within the planned dates. Recording an interview that did not happen is a false record.
std
III.B
When the audit team arrives, the main production line is down for unplanned maintenance and is expected to restart in the afternoon. What should the lead auditor do?
Base the production findings on records alone, since the line cannot be seen in operation this morning
End the audit and reschedule the full visit for a later date when production is running normally
Ask the auditee to restart the line early so the team can keep to the original morning schedule
Audit maintenance records and support processes now, and observe production once the line restarts
A lead auditor reshuffles the sequence to use the time well and still observes the process when it runs. Pressing the auditee to restart early could create a safety or quality problem of its own.
std
III.B
On a two-day audit, the lead auditor plans a short meeting with the auditee's guide at the end of day one. What is its main purpose?
To present the final audit conclusion and formally close the audit
To report progress and concerns and confirm tomorrow's schedule
To let the guide approve which findings the team will report
To collect the auditee's corrective actions for each finding
A daily briefing keeps the auditee informed and lets logistics be settled for the next day. The auditee does not approve findings, and the conclusion comes at the closing meeting.
std
III.C
A supervisor says mildly, "I don't think that is actually a requirement." What is the best first response?
Restate the requirement firmly and move on to the next checklist question
Agree to drop the point, since the disagreement is minor and not worth time
Ask which procedure he follows and show him where the requirement comes from
Note the remark and raise his attitude with management at the closing meeting

A mild disagreement is usually settled by asking questions and pointing to the source of the requirement. Restating it firmly without explanation tends to harden a disagreement that could have been cleared up.
std
III.C
While a finding is being discussed, a department manager raises his voice and accuses the auditor of trying to get his team in trouble. What should the auditor do?
Keep reading the requirement aloud until he lets her finish speaking
Withdraw the finding so the audit can continue without further conflict
