Leave the site and report the outburst to the audit client right away
Suggest a short break and return to the finding once things are calm
A severe, emotional disagreement calls for a cool-down period before the facts can be discussed. Withdrawing a finding that the evidence supports gives up objectivity to avoid conflict.
std
III.C
On a one-day audit, the guide has arranged a two-hour plant tour and a presentation on company history at the start of the day. How should the lead auditor view this?
As a courtesy that should be accepted in full to build rapport with the auditee
As useful audit evidence about the process approach used across the whole site
As grounds to end the audit early and report that the auditee will not cooperate
As a possible delaying tactic that eats into audit time and should be cut short

Long tours and presentations are a classic way to reduce the time left for real audit work. A short orientation is fine, but two hours on a one-day audit should be trimmed politely back toward the plan.
std
III.C
Records the auditor asked for at 9:00 a.m. are still "being located" at 2:00 p.m., and the guide keeps proposing long breaks. What is the best response?
Remind the management representative of the agreed plan and set a firm deadline
Wait patiently for the records, since the auditee controls when they are produced
Record a nonconformity for each missing record before seeing whether they exist
Remove those records from the scope so the rest of the plan can be finished

Pointing back to the plan agreed at the opening meeting and setting a clear deadline addresses delaying tactics without accusing anyone. Writing nonconformities before checking whether the records exist is not evidence-based.
std
III.C
An auditor is interviewing an operator, but the operator's supervisor keeps stepping in to answer. What should the auditor do?
Politely ask to hear from the operator, offering to talk with the supervisor later
Record the supervisor's answers as the operator's, since they describe the same job
End the interview and note that the operator could not answer the questions
Ask the supervisor to leave the building for the rest of the operator interview

The auditor manages the interruption courteously so the evidence comes from the person doing the work. Ending the interview misrepresents what happened, and the operator never had a fair chance to answer.
std
III.C
During an interview, a quality manager answers several phone calls and twice leaves the room. What is the best response?
Carry on with the questions while he is on the phone, so no audit time is wasted
Agree on a time to talk without phone calls, and reschedule the interview if needed
Record that he declined to take part in the audit and move on to another process
Ask his assistant to answer the remaining questions on his behalf from the office
Interruptions are handled by agreeing on conditions for an uninterrupted conversation. Recording that he declined is not what happened and turns a logistics issue into a false finding.
std
III.C
An auditor asks for "the training records" and is handed a binder of every training record in the plant from the last ten years. What should she do?
Work through the whole binder, since the auditee gave what she asked for
Record that the auditee is obstructing the audit with excess paperwork
Ask the auditee to choose a few records that they think are typical
Restate the request, naming the people, jobs and period she needs
A vague request invites an unhelpful answer, so the fix is to clarify it. Letting the auditee pick the sample undermines its objectivity.
std
III.C
A production manager argues each finding as soon as it is raised, slowing the audit. What is the best approach?
Stop raising findings with him and save all of them for the written report
Remind him of the process agreed at the opening meeting for discussing findings
Debate each finding on the spot until he agrees with it, however long that takes
Report his behavior to his manager as a refusal to cooperate with the audit

Reiterating the ground rules set at the opening meeting, including when findings are reviewed, keeps the audit on track without hiding anything. Saving every finding for the report means the auditee first sees them in writing, with no chance to review the evidence.
std
III.C
An auditee refuses to let the auditor into a storage area that is inside the agreed scope. After explaining why access is needed, the auditor still is not allowed in. What should he do next?
Inform the audit client and top management, and record the limitation
Enter the storage area anyway once the escort has left for the day
Drop the area from the scope quietly, since the auditee did not want it
Write a major nonconformity against the storage area's own procedures

When a conflict cannot be settled at the working level, the auditor involves a higher authority and documents the limit on scope. A nonconformity against the area's procedures cannot be raised without evidence from that area.
std
III.C
In which situation is a cool-down period the most fitting technique?
An operator is unsure of the answer and asks to check a procedure
A manager becomes visibly angry and stops responding to questions
An auditee asks what a clause of the standard means in practice
A supervisor politely disagrees about how a finding is worded
Cool-down periods suit heated, emotional situations where discussion has broken down. The other cases are handled with clarifying, explaining or asking questions.
std
III.C
A buyer says, "We don't do receiving inspection on that part. The customer waived it." What is the auditor's best next step?
Accept the statement and move on to the next part number on the list
Raise a nonconformity because receiving inspection was not performed
Ask the buyer's manager whether the buyer is telling the truth about this
Ask to see the waiver or written customer agreement
A well-aimed question for the supporting evidence settles the matter either way. Raising a nonconformity before checking whether a valid waiver exists could be wrong.
std
III.D
Which item is most important to cover at the opening meeting?
Presenting the issues already found in the document review as nonconformities
Giving a detailed walk-through of every checklist question the team will ask
Confirming the scope, the plan and how findings will be communicated
Asking the auditee which areas they would like the team to skip this time
The opening meeting confirms the arrangements so the audit runs with no surprises. Presenting findings before on-site evidence is gathered is premature.
std
III.D
The site's senior managers have 15 minutes for the closing meeting. How should the lead auditor structure it?
Read each finding aloud in the order the team found them, so nothing gets left out
Lead with the conclusion and major findings, then add detail as the time allows
Spend most of the time on positive practices, leaving the findings for the report
Postpone the closing meeting until the managers can give it a full two hours
Managers need the conclusion and the most significant issues first; detail can follow or be referenced. Holding back findings for the report denies the auditee the chance to hear and question them.
std
III.D
Midway through an audit, the auditor finds that product failing a safety test is being packed for shipment. What is the best action?
Note the finding and present it at the closing meeting with the others
Call an ad hoc meeting with the auditee's management right away
Stop the shipment herself by tagging the product as nonconforming
Tell the operators packing the product to stop and quarantine it

A serious, immediate risk should be communicated as soon as it is found through an ad hoc meeting so the auditee can act. Auditors do not take control of product themselves; that responsibility belongs to the auditee.
std
III.D
A lead auditor must report the same audit to the plant's process engineers and to the division vice president. Which approach is best?
Give both groups the same full-length report, so the two audiences receive exactly the same information
Give the vice president the detailed evidence for each process, since executives have the final say on action
Give the vice president risks and trends, and the engineers detailed evidence by process
Give the engineers a one-page summary of risks, since they will rework the details for the vice president
Managerial reporting stresses overall conclusions, risk and trends; technical reporting gives the evidence needed to act on specific processes. One full report for both serves neither audience well.
std
III.D
A lead auditor wants to show management which processes produced most of the findings across six audits. Which chart is best?
A run chart of findings by audit date
A pie chart of findings by auditor name
A Pareto chart of findings by process
A scatter diagram of findings and audit hours
A Pareto chart ranks categories so the few processes with most findings stand out. A run chart shows change over time, not which process contributes most.
std
III.D
An audit program manager wants to show whether the number of open corrective actions has been rising or falling over the past year. Which display is best?
A line chart of open corrective actions by month
A Pareto chart of corrective actions by clause number
A histogram of days each action stayed open
A cause-and-effect diagram of late actions
A line (run) chart shows direction over time, which is the question asked. A histogram shows how the ages are distributed, not whether the total is trending.
std
III.D
An auditor needs to show the auditee where in the order-to-shipment process several related findings occurred. Which is most effective?
A bar chart that compares the number of findings in each department
A process flow diagram with each finding marked at its step
A table that lists each finding in order of the clause it references
A control chart of the number of findings per process step per day

A flow diagram puts the findings in the context of the process, so the auditee can see where problems cluster and how they connect. A clause-ordered table shows nothing about where in the flow they arose.
std
III.D
An auditor's draft finding reads, "The careless operator on line 3 didn't bother to record the readings." What is the best revision?
"The operator on line 3 needs retraining on recording torque readings correctly."
"Line 3 shows a poor attitude toward recording torque readings in general."
"Torque readings for 4 of 10 sampled lots on line 3 were not recorded per WI-12."
"Torque recording on line 3 is not done properly and should be fixed soon."
Written findings should state the evidence and the requirement factually, without blame or opinion. Prescribing retraining also assumes a cause and a fix, which is the auditee's job to determine.
std
III.D
While presenting findings orally to a group of shop supervisors, the auditor sees confused looks when she uses terms like "objective evidence" and "conformity." What should she do?
Keep using the terms, since they are the standard terms of the profession
Hand out a glossary and continue the presentation without slowing down
Switch to plain terms with an example, then check that the group follows
Shorten the presentation and refer the group to the written report later
Effective oral communication adjusts to the audience and checks for understanding. A glossary with no pause does not fix the confusion while she is speaking.
std
III.D
An auditor plans to email the draft audit report to the auditee. What is the most appropriate practice?
Copy everyone who attended the opening meeting, so the report reaches all of them
Send it only to the agreed recipients, using the method agreed for confidential material
Post it to the shared drive the auditee's staff use so that everyone can read it
Send it from a personal email account in case the company system blocks the file

Electronic communication has to protect the confidentiality of audit information, so distribution and method follow what was agreed with the client. The attendance list is not the same as the authorized distribution list.
std
III.D
A closing meeting is being held at a supplier abroad where most managers speak English as a second language. Which approach is best?
Speak faster than usual so there is time to repeat any points that are not understood
Rely on slides with full paragraphs of text, so the managers can read along as you speak
Use the same informal phrasing that goes over well with domestic audiences at home
Speak plainly without idioms, leave a written summary, and use an interpreter if needed
With a global audience, plain language, a written summary and interpretation where needed reduce misunderstanding. Domestic idioms and informal phrasing are the things most likely to be lost.
std
III.D
An opening meeting will be held by video with participants at the auditee's site and two auditors in another time zone. What is the most important preparation?
Test the platform, send the agenda and plan ahead, and agree how records will be shown
Rely on the auditee to sort out any technical problems once the meeting is underway
Skip the opening meeting and email the plan, since remote audits do not need one
Hold the meeting at a convenient hour for the auditors, whatever the site's local time
Remote meetings depend on working technology and clear advance arrangements, including how documents will be shown. An opening meeting is still needed in a remote audit.
std
III.D
A lead auditor reports a corporate audit that covered four sites. Which way of presenting the results is most useful to corporate management?
One combined list of findings with the site names removed to protect the sites
Results for each site plus a combined view of issues common to several
Four separate site reports with no comparison drawn between the sites at all
Only the findings from the site that had the most findings during the audit
A multi-site report should support action at each site and show systemic issues that cut across sites. Separate reports with no comparison hide the patterns corporate management most needs to see.
std
III.E
Which question is open-ended?
"How do you know which drawing revision to use?"
"Do you check the drawing revision each time you start?"
"Is the current drawing posted at the station?"
"Was this drawing revision issued in March?"
Open-ended questions invite the person to explain in their own words. The other options can each be answered with yes, no or a single fact.
std
III.E
When is a closed question most useful in an audit interview?
To open the interview and get the person talking about how the job is done
To understand why the operator chose a different method from the procedure
To confirm a specific fact, such as whether the gauge was checked before the run
To learn how the department decides which jobs to run first on each shift
Closed questions are efficient for pinning down a specific fact once the context is known. Understanding how or why something is done calls for open questions.
std
III.E
An auditor asks, "Do you follow the procedure?" and the operator answers, "Yes." What is the best next question?
"Are you sure you follow every single step of it?"
"Has anyone ever told you not to follow it?"
"So you follow the procedure every time?"
"Can you walk me through how you set up this job?"
An open question shifts from a yes answer to a description the auditor can compare with the procedure. The other options are still closed and invite the same one-word reply.
std
III.E
Which behavior best shows active listening during an audit interview?
Asking follow-up questions based on what the person just said
Working out the next checklist question while the person talks
Finishing the person's sentences to keep the interview moving
Keeping eyes on the checklist so no question is missed
Active listening means attending to what is said and building on it. Planning the next question while the person speaks means the auditor is not really listening.
std
III.E
An operator gives a long description of how failed parts are reworked. Which reply is an example of paraphrasing?
"So failed parts are reworked and retested before returning to the line, right?"
"Thank you for explaining all of that. Could you show me the rework procedure document now, please?"
"That sounds like a complicated process to manage. How long have you been doing rework on this line?"
"I will note in my records that parts failing the leak test go to the rework area for repair."
Paraphrasing restates the person's point in the listener's words and invites correction, which confirms understanding. Noting it in records without checking back skips that confirmation.
std
III.E
An inspector says she is worried that whatever she says will get her coworkers in trouble. Which response shows empathy?
"There is nothing to worry about, so please just answer the questions as completely as possible."
"If you are worried about your coworkers, then maybe there is a problem I should know about here."
"I can stop the interview now and ask your supervisor the remaining questions on the checklist."
"I understand the concern. I'm looking at how the process works, and findings won't name anyone."
Empathy acknowledges the person's feelings and addresses the concern behind them. Brushing the worry aside or treating it as a sign of wrongdoing makes her less likely to speak openly.
std
III.E
A supervisor says all operators are trained, but he looks away, crosses his arms and hesitates before answering. What should the auditor do?
Record a nonconformity, since his body language shows the answer is false
Accept his answer, since body language is not objective audit evidence
Tell him directly that he appears to be hiding something from the audit
Treat it as a cue to verify the claim by sampling training records

Non-verbal cues are a signal to probe further, not evidence on their own. Accepting the answer without checking ignores a useful warning sign, and recording a nonconformity from body language has no evidence behind it.
std
III.E
After the auditor asks an open question, the technician is silent for several seconds. What is the best response?
Rephrase it as a yes-or-no question to help him
Wait a little longer so he can think and answer
Move on, since the silence suggests he doesn't know
Offer a likely answer and ask if that's what he meant
A pause often means the person is thinking, and waiting gives a more complete answer. Supplying an answer leads the witness and taints the evidence.
std
III.E
A planner explains the first half of the scheduling process and then stops. Which prompt is best?
"Then you update the master schedule, don't you?"
"I assume that's where the problems start, right?"
"Is that everything you do in the process?"
"What happens after that?"
A neutral prompt keeps the person talking without suggesting the answer. A leading prompt plants the auditor's expectation in the reply.
std
III.E
An operator's supervisor insists on staying for the interview, and the operator glances at him before every answer. What should the auditor do?
Continue as normal, since the supervisor has a right to hear what his operators tell the auditor
Direct all remaining questions to the supervisor, since the operator seems unsure of the answers
Explain that this is routine and ask to speak with the operator alone for part of the interview
Note in the report that the operator's answers were influenced by the supervisor and move on

A supervisor's presence can shape what an operator says, so the auditor prompts for a private conversation, explained as routine rather than as distrust. Recording undue influence as a conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
std
III.E
An auditor interviews three inspectors together, and one of them answers every question. What should the auditor do?
Let the most talkative inspector answer for the group, since he seems to know best
End the group interview and write down that the other two could not answer
Direct questions to each inspector in turn about the steps that person performs
Ask the talkative inspector to leave so the others can speak more freely

In a group interview the auditor must make sure each person's practice is heard, which is done by directing questions to individuals. Recording that the others could not answer is unfair when they were never asked.
std
III.E
An auditor must interview operators through a translator. Which practice is best?
Use the area supervisor as translator, since he knows the process and the people who run it
Ask long, combined questions so that the total number of translations is kept to a minimum
Speak mainly to the translator rather than to the operator to keep the interview efficient
Use an independent translator and short questions, and check that answers are relayed in full
Short, single-topic questions and a translator with no stake in the area keep the evidence accurate. A supervisor as translator may filter or soften what the operators say.
std
III.F
At the kickoff for a five-person audit team, what best ensures clear roles and equitable treatment of team members?
Letting team members choose the processes they prefer, first come, first served, to keep morale high
Assigning each auditor's duties in writing, balanced by workload, and reviewing them as a team
Giving the most experienced auditors the full workload so the newer auditors can simply observe them
Keeping the assignments flexible and unwritten so the lead auditor can change them at any time
Written, balanced assignments reviewed with the team make roles clear and treat members fairly. A first-come approach leaves the workload and fit to chance.
std
III.F
On past audits, team members handed in findings in different formats and at different times, which delayed the report. What should the lead auditor do on the next audit?
Collect whatever each auditor produces and reformat it all herself afterward
Ask the auditee to compile the team's findings into a single report document
State up front what each auditor must deliver, in what format and by when
Drop the written findings and rely only on the notes from the closing meeting
Clear direction on deliverables prevents rework and delay. Having the auditee compile the findings compromises the independence of the report.
std
III.F
On arrival, one auditor cannot enter the clean room because he has not completed the site's gowning training. What should the lead auditor have done during planning?
Assign only auditors who already work in clean rooms to every audit on the program
Confirm the access, safety and training needs for each area and arrange them in advance
Leave site access needs for the auditee's guide to arrange on the morning of the audit
Remove the clean room from the audit scope, since access always causes delays like this

Team building includes identifying the resources each auditor needs, such as access, safety equipment and training, and making sure they are available. Leaving it to the morning of the audit invites this exact delay.
std
III.F
An auditor-in-training on the team keeps asking leading questions in interviews. What is the best way for the lead auditor to coach her?
Give specific feedback in private afterward and model better questions
Correct her in front of the auditee the moment a leading question is asked
Take over all of her interviews for the rest of the audit without explanation
Wait until the audit is over and mention it in her written performance review
Coaching works best when feedback is timely, specific and private, backed by example. Correcting her in front of the auditee damages her credibility and the team's.
std
III.F
Two auditors on the team disagree on whether a record supports a nonconformity. What should the lead auditor do?
Go with the auditor who has more years of experience on audit teams
Ask the auditee which of the two views they think is the correct one
Drop the finding, since the team could not agree on it among themselves
Review the evidence against the requirement with both of them and then decide
Conflicts between members over findings are settled by going back to the evidence and the requirement, with the lead auditor deciding. Seniority alone is not a basis for a finding.
std
III.F
In daily team meetings, a newer auditor rarely speaks even though she covers important areas. What should the lead auditor do?
Assume she has nothing to report unless she speaks up herself
Ask each member in turn to report observations and concerns
Have her email her notes after each meeting has finished instead
Report her areas himself, using her working papers from the day
Going around the table gives every member a structured chance to contribute. Assuming silence means nothing to report risks missing important information.
std
III.F
A team member wants to write a finding based on an operator's complaint that management ignores safety concerns. What should the lead auditor do?
Let him record it, since operators know best what happens on the floor
Tell him to drop it, since operator complaints are outside the audit scope
Record it as an observation using the operator's own words and name
Ask what evidence supports it and have it verified before it is recorded
Fostering objectivity means findings rest on verified evidence, not one person's view. Dropping it outright could miss a real issue that verification might confirm.
std
III.F
How should the lead auditor monitor the team's progress during a three-day audit?
Wait for the final day and count the findings each auditor has written
Ask the auditee's guide each evening how well each auditor is doing
Check whether each auditor has written at least one finding every day
Compare each auditor's coverage with the plan at daily team meetings
Checking coverage against the plan each day lets the lead auditor find gaps while there is still time to fix them. Counting findings measures output, not whether the scope is covered.
std
III.F
An audit team must agree on its overall conclusion, and members see the evidence differently. Which outcome represents consensus?
Every member's first choice is exactly the same conclusion after the evidence has been discussed
More than half of the team members vote in favor of the conclusion after the discussion has ended
Every member can accept and support the conclusion, even if it was not his or her own first choice
The lead auditor chooses the conclusion after the discussion, and the others are told to accept it
Consensus is reached when all members can live with and support the decision after their views are heard. A majority vote is a different method that can leave members unconvinced.
std
III.F
Why should a lead auditor build a team with different backgrounds, such as quality, engineering and finance?
Different viewpoints help the team spot more risks and test each other's conclusions
A mixed team needs less planning, since each member already knows what to look for
A mixed team reaches agreement faster, since members rarely disagree with each other
Different viewpoints let the lead auditor skip technical experts on complex processes
Diverse perspectives widen what the team notices and challenge weak conclusions. Diverse teams usually need more facilitation to reach agreement, not less.
std
III.F
A newly assembled audit team is polite, cautious and looks to the lead auditor for direction on almost everything. Which stage of team development is this?
Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
Forming is marked by politeness, uncertainty about roles and reliance on the leader. Storming follows when members start to challenge one another and the leader.
std
III.F
On day one, two auditors argue about who should audit purchasing, and one questions the lead auditor's plan. What stage is the team in, and what should the lead auditor do?
Forming; give the team more time to get to know one another before acting
Norming; let the team settle the matter itself without the leader stepping in
Storming; address the conflict openly and restate the roles and the reasons for them
Performing; delegate the assignment decision to the two auditors involved
Challenges to roles and the leader mark storming, which calls for open handling of conflict and clear roles. Leaving it to settle on its own risks the conflict spilling into the audit.
std
III.F
By the second day, team members have agreed on a common format for findings and are starting to accept one another's working styles. Which stage is this?
Forming
Adjourning
Norming
Storming
Agreeing on shared ways of working and accepting each other marks norming. Storming is the earlier stage of conflict over roles and approach.
std
III.F
A long-standing audit team works with little supervision, shares information freely and solves scheduling problems on its own. What is the best leadership approach at this stage?
Give detailed instructions for each task to keep the team on course
Reassign roles to restart the team's development from the beginning
Hold longer daily meetings to settle disputes over the team's roles
Delegate and step back, monitoring results instead of directing tasks
A performing team works best when the leader delegates and supports rather than directs. Detailed direction suits forming, not a team that already runs itself.
std
III.F
After the final report is issued, the lead auditor meets the team to recognize contributions and capture lessons for future audits. Which stage of team development does this reflect?
Performing
Adjourning
Norming
Forming
Adjourning is the closing stage, when the team's work is wrapped up, contributions are recognized and the team disbands. Performing describes the productive work phase before that.
std
IV.A.1
Department heads at a plant often cancel internal audits at short notice, and nobody challenges them. What is the most effective step for top management to take?
Have the lead auditor reschedule each cancelled audit with the same department head who cancelled it
Cut the number of scheduled audits so fewer of them end up being cancelled
Set a policy that gives the audit program authority and expects managers to take part
Let auditors arrive unannounced so departments have no chance to cancel
Cancellations persist because the audit function lacks a mandate that managers must respect, and only top management can grant it. Rescheduling with the same people leaves the cause untouched.
std
IV.A.1
Which action by senior management best shows ongoing support for an established audit function?
Writing the audit checklists so they match what management wants found
Approving which findings auditors may include in each final report
Reviewing results and resourcing the agreed actions
Placing the audit coordinator under the production manager
Support means providing resources and acting on what audits reveal. Approving or shaping findings undermines the objectivity the function depends on.
std
IV.A.1
Why should the internal audit function report to a level of management above the areas it audits?
To protect independence and give findings enough weight to be acted on
To let senior managers decide which nonconformities are written up in reports
To pay auditors from the same budget as the departments they audit
To give the audit function authority to release product for shipment
Reporting above the audited areas keeps auditors free from pressure by those areas and ensures results reach someone who can act. Letting managers filter findings would defeat that purpose.
std
IV.A.1
A quality manager is launching a new internal audit program. What should she secure from top management first?
A list of the problems management expects the auditors to find
Agreement to audit only the departments that ask to be audited
Sign-off on the personal performance goals of each auditor
Defined objectives, scope, authority and resources
Top management establishes the program by setting its objectives and scope, assigning authority and providing resources. Expecting particular findings biases the audits before they start.
std
IV.A.2

An audit program has 24 internal audits a year. Each audit uses two auditors, and each auditor needs 6 h to plan, 14 h on site and 4 h to report and follow up. How many auditor-hours should the budget hold?
576 hours
672 hours
960 hours
1,152 hours
Each auditor needs 6 + 14 + 4 = 24 h, so 24 audits × 2 auditors × 24 h = 1,152 h. 576 h forgets the second auditor, and 960 h leaves out reporting and follow-up time.
std
IV.A.2
An audit manager builds next year's audit budget from auditor hours alone. What significant cost has been left out?
Registrar fees for the next third-party certification audit at the site
Depreciation on the gauges used on the production floor
Salaries of quality staff who are not qualified as auditors
Time auditees spend preparing, being interviewed and closing actions
Internal audits take time from the people audited, and a sound budget accounts for it. Registrar fees belong to the external certification budget, not the internal audit staffing plan.
std
IV.A.2
A company's only qualified internal auditor must audit a specialized heat-treating process she has no experience with. Which arrangement fits best?
Contract a qualified auditor or expert for that audit
Have her audit it alone using the general system checklist
Skip the process until an internal auditor can be trained in it
Ask the heat-treat supervisor to audit his own process this time
Contracting fills a competence gap without losing coverage or independence. Self-audit by the supervisor gives up independence, and skipping leaves a special process unchecked.
std
IV.A.2
A buyer needs to audit a medium-risk supplier on another continent, and travel would cost more than the rest of the audit. Which approach is most reasonable?
Use a contracted local auditor or a remote audit, matched to the risk
Remove the supplier from the audit schedule for good
Send two auditors so that the long travel effort is shared between them
Delay the audit until a trip to that region is planned
Cost and geography are valid reasons to change how an audit is done, but not to drop coverage of a medium-risk supplier. Sending two auditors raises the cost problem rather than solving it.
std
IV.A.2
Three device makers use the same sterilization contractor and each audits it every year against the same standard. What would most reduce total cost while keeping coverage?
Each customer auditing once every three years with no other checks
A shared audit whose report all three accept
The contractor completing a checklist and mailing it to each customer
Each customer shortening its own audit to half a day on site
A shared audit covers the same requirements once for all the customers, cutting cost for everyone, including the contractor. Shortening each audit saves money by losing coverage.
std
IV.A.2

A site certified to quality, environmental and safety management standards runs three separate audit programs. Auditees complain about repeat visits on the same topics. What should the audit manager evaluate?
Integrated audits covering all three systems
Dropping the environmental audits because they overlap with safety
Letting auditees send junior staff to the repeat interviews
Moving all three programs into the same month of the year
Integrated audits remove duplicate effort on shared elements such as document control and management review while keeping each system covered. Dropping a whole system loses required coverage.
std
IV.A.2
The paint line has had major findings in four straight audits, while the warehouse has had none in three years. How should the audit manager adjust resources?
Keep both areas on the same frequency so the schedule stays fair
Stop auditing the warehouse and move its auditor to production
Shift audit time toward the paint line and audit the warehouse less often
Hire more auditors so both areas can receive more audit time
Results should steer resources to where risk and problems are. Equal frequency ignores the evidence, and hiring adds cost without fixing the poor allocation.
std
IV.A.2
Audits in a program routinely overrun their dates, and reports go out weeks late. When reviewing the staffing budget, what should the audit manager check first?
Whether planning and reporting time was budgeted
Whether auditors are writing too many findings per audit
Whether auditees are being told about audits too far ahead
Whether the report template has too many required fields
Budgets that count only on-site time squeeze planning and reporting, which shows up as overruns and late reports. Cutting findings to save time would harm audit quality.
std
IV.A.3
Which set best describes the minimum an internal quality auditor needs before leading an audit?
An outside auditor certification and at least ten years with the organization
Expert-level knowledge of every process the auditor may be assigned to audit
Supervisory authority over the people working in the areas to be audited
Audit principles, the criteria and enough process knowledge to judge evidence

A competent auditor needs audit methods, the criteria and enough grasp of the process to weigh evidence. Expert knowledge of every process is not a minimum requirement; technical experts can fill gaps.
std
IV.A.3
A newly trained auditor writes findings that give opinions but cite no evidence or requirement. What training gap is most likely?
Knowledge of the industry regulations that apply to the site
Facilitation skills for opening and closing meetings
Collecting objective evidence and citing criteria
Awareness of cultural differences in the audited workforce
Findings must link evidence to a requirement, which is core audit process training. Regulatory knowledge would help with criteria but does not explain unsupported opinions.
std
IV.A.3
Internal auditors with automotive parts experience are assigned to audit a new pharmaceutical packaging line. What training is most essential before they start?
A refresher course on general audit principles and the audit cycle
The regulations and standards for that industry
Advanced statistics so they can reanalyze the line's process data
Lean methods so they can suggest waste reduction on the line
Auditors already know how to audit; what they lack is the criteria of a regulated new industry. A general audit refresher repeats what they know.
std
IV.A.3
At a unionized plant, operators decline to answer an auditor's questions until their union steward is present. What should the auditor do?
Record the refusal as a nonconformity against the site's training process
Interview the supervisor instead and close out that area of the audit
Respect the arrangement and resume the interviews once the steward joins
Ask the operators to answer informally and off the record for now
Organized labor agreements shape how people may take part, and respecting them keeps the audit constructive. Writing a nonconformity for exercising a labor right is not based on any audit criterion.
std
IV.A.3
An auditor audits a site where openly questioning a senior person is seen as rude. Interviewees give short answers that agree with everything. What is the auditor's best adjustment?
Accept the agreeing answers as evidence that the processes conform
Hold private, open-ended interviews and confirm answers with records and observation
Ask sharper, more pointed questions in group meetings until people begin to give details
State in the report that the site staff did not cooperate with the audit
Cultural norms can suppress candid answers, so the auditor changes the setting and verifies by other means. Accepting polite agreement as evidence mistakes courtesy for conformity.
std
IV.A.3
Two auditee managers start arguing in a closing meeting about which of them owns a finding. What is the best facilitation response?
Withdraw the finding so the meeting can end on a cordial note
Refocus on the evidence and leave ownership to their management
Assign the finding to whichever manager appears more senior
End the meeting at once and issue the report without discussion
A good facilitator keeps attention on facts and the requirement, and ownership of action belongs to the auditee's management. Withdrawing a valid finding to avoid conflict compromises the audit.
std
IV.A.3
A company qualifies internal auditors after a three-day course and sets no further requirements. What is the main weakness in this approach?
A three-day course is longer than an internal auditor needs
Auditors should hold an outside auditor certification before they start auditing
Nothing keeps auditor competence current through ongoing practice and training
Only the lead auditor in each audit team needs qualification
Competence fades and criteria change, so qualification should require continuing education and regular audit practice. Outside certification is not a requirement for internal auditors.
std
IV.A.3
A young auditor notices that senior operators give her curt answers and direct their replies to her older male co-auditor. What is the best way to handle this?
Let the co-auditor take over all of the interviews with senior operators
Stay professional, keep her role and agree on roles with her co-auditor
Write a finding about the operators' attitude toward the audit team
Stop the audit and report the operators to the plant manager

Age and gender can affect how auditees respond, and a planned, professional approach keeps the audit on track without giving up her role. Handing over every interview concedes to the bias and weakens the team.
std
IV.A.4
Which metric best shows whether an internal audit program is effective rather than just busy?
Trend in repeat findings after corrective actions were closed
Number of audits completed on time against the approved yearly schedule
Average number of findings written in each audit
Hours of auditor training completed during the year
Falling repeat findings show audits are leading to lasting fixes. Schedule completion counts activity and says nothing about results.
std
IV.A.4
Management asks how the audit program affects the bottom line. Which measure answers this most directly?
Number of auditor days spent on site over the last year
Percentage of audit reports issued within the target time
Auditee satisfaction scores taken from post-audit surveys
Failure costs avoided by audit actions versus program cost
The bottom-line question is about money, so it needs savings set against cost. On-time reports and satisfaction scores describe how the program runs, not what it returns.
std
IV.A.4
Which measure best shows the audit program's effect on the organization's risk level?
Total number of findings recorded across the whole program in each quarter
Number of audits performed in low-risk support departments
Change in the number of high-risk processes with open major findings
Share of auditors who hold an outside certification
Fewer high-risk processes carrying unresolved major findings means exposure has dropped. A raw finding count mixes trivial and serious issues and can move for many reasons.
std
IV.A.4
An audit program reports 100% schedule completion every year, yet customer complaints keep rising. What does this most suggest?
The complaint data is suspect, because the audits themselves found no issues
The metric tracks activity, not whether audits find and fix real risks
More audits should be added until they match the complaint rate
The program is working and the complaints have unrelated causes
Completion shows audits happened, not that they were aimed well or led to improvement; rising complaints point to that gap. Doubting the complaint data puts too much faith in a weak metric.
std
IV.A.5
A plant is writing its first internal audit procedure. Which content is most essential?
A list of the nonconformities found at the plant in the past year
The names and pay grades of each currently qualified auditor
How audits are planned, run, reported and followed up, and by whom
Fixed checklists for every process that are never to be revised
The procedure defines the audit process and responsibilities so audits are consistent. Fixed, never-revised checklists would stop the program from adapting.
std
IV.A.5
Which approach to setting the annual internal audit schedule best supports the organization's objectives?
Audit every process once a year, working through them in alphabetical order
Audit only the areas that ask the quality team for help
Rotate the three processes that are easiest to reach
Set frequency by importance, risk, changes and past results
Weighting the schedule by importance, risk and history puts audit effort where it matters most. A flat annual cycle is simple but ignores where problems are likely.
std
IV.A.5
An audit manager reviews the internal audit program only when the certification body raises a concern. What would better support the organization?
A review held only when the audit budget is reduced
A set review cycle, such as quarterly, to adjust the plan
Each auditor reviewing only the audits he or she led
Holding all changes until the next annual management review
A regular review cycle lets the program respond to results and changes during the year. Waiting for the annual review delays action that the data may already call for.
std
IV.A.5
Across 12 internal audits, six departments have findings about using obsolete drawings. What should the audit manager recommend?
Review document control as a systemic cause
Have each department retrain its own staff on drawing use
Raise the audit frequency in those six departments
Close each finding on its own as departments respond
The same problem in many areas points to a shared process, here document control. Department-by-department fixes treat symptoms and leave the source in place.
std
IV.A.5
A company brings in a new contract manufacturer and a new ERP system in the same year. How should the internal audit program respond?
Keep the approved schedule as is until the next annual cycle
Add audits covering the new risks this year
Wait until problems appear before auditing either change
Accept the ERP vendor's tests in place of an audit
Major changes create emerging risks, and the schedule should be revised to address them. Waiting until the next cycle leaves the changes unchecked when they are most likely to fail.
std
IV.A.5
A periodic program review shows most findings are closed by retraining, and the same issues keep coming back. Which system enhancement should the audit manager recommend?
Require verified root cause analysis before corrective actions can be closed
Lengthen the retraining sessions that are given each time a finding is raised
Raise the severity rating of any finding that happens to recur
Have auditors write the corrective actions for the auditees
Recurrence after retraining shows causes are not being found, so the closure process needs a root cause step. Longer retraining repeats the action that already failed.
std
IV.A.6
A company is writing the procedure for its supplier audit program. Which element is most important to include?
Criteria for which suppliers are audited and how often
A rule that every approved supplier is audited on site each quarter
A requirement that suppliers pay for every audit
A list of suppliers who have failed past audits
Risk- and performance-based selection criteria let limited audit resources go to the suppliers that matter. Auditing everyone every quarter wastes effort on low-risk suppliers.
std
IV.A.6
Before approving a new casting supplier, a buyer sends a questionnaire and then visits the site to evaluate its quality system and process capability. This is best described as a:
Supplier surveillance audit
Supplier self-assessment
Finished product audit
Supplier qualification survey
Evaluating a prospective supplier before approval is a qualification survey. Surveillance audits come after approval, to confirm controls are maintained.
std
IV.A.6
A supplier approved two years ago has shipped good parts since. What is the main purpose of a surveillance audit there?
Re-qualify the supplier from scratch as if it were a new source
Check whether the supplier's prices are still competitive
Decide whether the supplier can receive confidential design data
Confirm approved controls are still working
Surveillance audits check that an approved supplier keeps its system and controls working over time. Repeating full qualification is unnecessary for a supplier with good history.
std
IV.A.6
A buyer has 300 low-risk suppliers but staff to audit only 30 a year. Which approach best extends coverage?
Audit 30 suppliers chosen at random and accept the rest without checks
Stop supplier audits and depend on incoming inspection alone
Use supplier self-assessments and audit those that raise concerns
Audit only the 30 suppliers with the highest annual spend
Self-assessments give some insight into every supplier and help target the limited on-site audits. Spend alone does not reflect quality risk.
std
IV.A.6
A key supplier's quality and delivery ratings have fallen for three quarters. Which supplier improvement step fits best?
Agree on an improvement plan with targets and support, then verify results
Move the business to a new supplier at once, without assessing the new source
Send a letter demanding better performance next quarter
Raise incoming inspection levels and take no other action
A joint plan with targets and follow-up addresses causes and keeps a key source. Extra inspection only screens out bad parts and leaves the cause in place.
std
IV.A.6
When setting the supplier audit schedule, which supplier should get the highest audit priority?
Long-time office supply vendor with no quality problems
Large packaging supplier with stable quality ratings
New supplier of shop rags used for general cleaning
Sole source of a safety-critical part with recent escapes
Criticality, lack of alternatives and recent escapes all raise risk, so this supplier comes first. A new supplier of a low-impact item carries little risk to product quality.
std
IV.A.7
An internal audit finds that one cell has nearly eliminated setup errors with a simple visual checklist. What should the audit program do with this?
Leave it out of the report, because audits should report only nonconformities
Require every cell to adopt it before the next scheduled audit
Report it as a good practice and recommend evaluating it for other cells
Record it as an opportunity for improvement in that same cell

Audits can identify good practices and recommend that the organization consider them elsewhere. Ordering immediate adoption skips checking whether it suits other cells, and audit reports are not limited to nonconformities.
std
IV.A.7
A good practice has been confirmed at one site. Which step best spreads it across the organization?
Build it into standard procedures and verify adoption in later audits
Email a description to the other sites and leave adoption up to each one
Recognize the site that developed it at the next awards event
Ask the originating site to keep refining it on its own
Standardizing and then verifying turns a local practice into an organizational one. An optional email rarely changes how other sites work.
std
IV.A.7
A recall traced to one plant reveals a weakness in how design changes reach the shop floor. What should the audit program do with this lesson?
Limit follow-up to the plant where the recall started
Wait until the other plants report similar problems before acting on it
Record it only in the closed recall file for that plant
Add checks for the same weakness to audit plans at the other plants
A lesson learned at one plant is a risk to check for elsewhere before it repeats. Waiting for reports invites the same failure at another site.
std
IV.A.7
Before calling a local practice a best practice in an audit report, what should the auditor confirm?
That the area manager considers it the best approach
That it is new and has not been seen at any of the other sites
Evidence that it gives better results than the usual method
That it was developed by the quality department
A best practice should be supported by results, not opinion or origin. The manager's view is not evidence of better performance.
std
IV.A.8
How does a well-run audit program lower an organization's risk level?
It shifts accountability for failures from managers to the auditors
It finds weak controls so they are fixed early
It removes the need for process owners to monitor their own processes
It ensures that no nonconforming product can reach a customer
Audits reduce risk by exposing control weaknesses so management can correct them in time. They do not replace process monitoring, and no audit program can guarantee zero escapes.
std
IV.A.8
A process recently had a serious customer escape and a change of process owner. How should this affect its audits?
Keep the normal schedule so the new owner can settle in first
Audit it sooner and more often until controls are shown to work
Remove it from the schedule while the escape is being investigated
Audit it less often because the escape is already getting attention
Higher risk calls for more frequent audits until effectiveness is shown. Pausing audits during an investigation leaves the riskiest process unchecked.
std
IV.A.8
A stable, low-risk process has been audited monthly for two years with no findings. What change does a risk-based approach support?
Keep monthly audits, since a clean record proves they work
Reduce its frequency and redirect the time
Stop auditing it entirely and rely on its clean history
Assign a newer auditor so the findings will increase
Audit frequency should follow risk and past results, so a stable record justifies fewer audits, not none. Ending audits altogether removes any check on future change.
std
IV.A.8
During an audit, an auditor learns that the plant's only source of a key resin is in a flood-prone area and there is no plan for losing it. Which area does this most concern?
Succession planning
Supplier self-assessment
Business continuity planning
Document and record control
Preparing for the loss of a critical input from a disaster is business continuity planning. Succession planning deals with replacing key people, not supply.
std
IV.A.8
A site has a written disaster recovery plan. Which evidence best shows the plan would work?
A signature from the site manager on the plan's cover page
A plan that addresses every disaster type the team could think of
Copies of the plan stored in each department's office
Test or drill records and actions taken on the gaps they found
Only testing shows whether a plan works, and acting on gaps shows it is maintained. An approved, well-distributed plan can still fail in use.
std
IV.A.8
The only engineer who knows how to set up a critical furnace retires next year, and no one else is trained. Which issue should the auditor raise?
Lack of disaster planning for loss of the building
No succession plan for critical knowledge
Overdue calibration of the furnace instruments
Weak supplier control over furnace spare parts
Depending on one person for critical know-how is a succession planning gap. Disaster planning addresses physical events, not the planned loss of a key person.
std
IV.A.9
Which audit program input would be most useful to a management review?
Full copies of every audit report issued during the review period
A short summary of trends, systemic issues and risk changes
A ranking of auditors by the number of findings each one wrote
Next period's audit schedule with no other supporting detail
Management needs analysis it can act on, not raw material. Full reports bury the important trends in detail.
std
IV.A.9
Over four quarters, total findings at a plant fell, but findings on supplier controls doubled. How should this go to management review?
Show the supplier control trend as a rising risk that needs action
Present the overall drop as proof that the system is improving
Hold the topic back until a full extra year of data is in hand
Give the raw totals only and let management draw its own conclusions
A rising trend within a falling total is exactly what management needs to see. Reporting only the overall drop hides a growing risk.
std
IV.A.9
Which item belongs in the audit program's input to management review as a change in risk?
A new regulation affecting processes that audits found weakly controlled
The total number of training hours the auditors logged during the review year
The audit team's preferred format for future reports
The list of audits that were completed on schedule
A new requirement landing on weak processes raises risk and calls for a management decision. Training hours and report format are program details, not risk changes.
std
IV.A.9
What most makes audit program input to management review meaningful?
It lists every finding together with the full supporting evidence
It reports only the findings that are still open at review time
It ties results to objectives and needed decisions
It avoids conclusions so that the audit function stays neutral
Input is useful when it connects results to objectives and points to decisions. Drawing evidence-based conclusions does not compromise independence.
std
IV.A.10
Auditing a lab's electronic test system, an auditor finds that results can be changed with no record of who changed them or why. What is the main concern?
Record retention, because old results may be lost
Data integrity, because there is no audit trail
Cybersecurity, because outsiders may reach the network
Calibration, because the test instruments may drift

Without an audit trail, nobody can tell whether results are original or altered, which is a data integrity failure. Retention concerns how long records are kept, not whether they can be silently edited.
std
IV.A.10
Which pattern in electronic inspection records should most alert an auditor to possible falsification?
Many results entered in a burst at shift end, all at exactly nominal
Results that vary from part to part inside the tolerance band around nominal
A few out-of-tolerance readings with recorded reinspection
Entries made by several inspectors at times across the shift
Real measurements vary, and batch entries timed after the work suggest values were filled in rather than measured. Normal variation and documented rejects are signs of honest data.
